# BIOSIM PROJECT HISTORY

Chronological log of completed milestones, moved out of `CLAUDE.md` on
2026-08-17 (process-improvement item Q3 -- `CLAUDE.md` had grown to
~14,900 lines, most of it this append-only history, making "what's true
right now" hard to separate from "what happened once"). `CLAUDE.md`
keeps architecture, known-bugs, current validation numbers, and current
priorities; this file keeps the full record of how each milestone was
reached. New completed-milestone entries should be appended to THIS file
going forward, not back into `CLAUDE.md` -- see `CLAUDE.md`'s own
"What does not change" paragraph for the current per-milestone
discipline (RED/GREEN, review passes, etc.); only the DONE-entry
destination has moved.

This file is split into two parts, matching two separate ranges moved
out of `CLAUDE.md`'s own file order -- Part 1 is the original "WHAT TO
BUILD NEXT (priority order)" section (Track 1 through the start of
Track 4/metabolism work); Part 2 continues immediately after (in real
chronological terms) but was separated in `CLAUDE.md`'s own file order
by the AGENT TOOLING section and the CITATION RE-AUDIT PROTOCOL's own
definition, both of which stayed in `CLAUDE.md` as standing reference
material, not history.

## Part 1

## WHAT TO BUILD NEXT (priority order)

### DONE — Consolidated `MealInput.DEFAULT_VG_L_PER_KG` onto the same literature-anchored value as the IVGTT fix
Follow-up to #17: that fix deliberately did NOT touch the oral-meal
constant (same uncited `0.286 L/kg`, shared across every meal
simulation) without a dedicated re-validation pass. Did that pass now,
properly, rather than leaving it flagged indefinitely:

1. **Checked the physics before touching anything.** IV and oral glucose
   both dilute into the same single glucose compartment (`G`) in this
   ODE -- there's no principled reason for the "mmol appearing ->
   concentration change" conversion factor to differ by route. Vg only
   scales `Ra(t)`'s *amplitude* (total dose), not its timing shape, which
   is set entirely by `k_emptying`/`k_absorption` -- confirmed directly
   by simulating GI=100 meals at `Vg=0.286/0.230/0.200` before changing
   anything: `time_to_peak_glucose_min` stayed ~49-50 min across all
   three (dose scale doesn't move a bi-exponential curve's peak time),
   only magnitude-based points moved. This meant `ogtt_calibrated_glucose()`'s
   `k_emptying`/`k_absorption` fit did NOT need re-fitting -- only the
   magnitude-tolerance benchmarks needed re-checking.
2. **Changed `DEFAULT_VG_L_PER_KG` to `0.230`** (same Mora-Gonzalez et
   al. 2024, PMID:38389141 citation as #17) and **re-ran the full OGTT
   benchmark suite**, not just one point, before accepting it:
   ```
   peak_glucose               -1.9%  -> +5.9%   (still PASS, NORMAL/25%)
   glucose_at_120min          -7.8%  -> -4.7%   (IMPROVED, still PASS)
   peak_insulin               -11.2% -> +1.2%   (IMPROVED substantially)
   time_to_peak_insulin_min   -5.1%  -> -9.1%   (still comfortably PASS, WIDE)
   time_to_peak_glucose_min   +10.9% -> +9.6%   (essentially unchanged)
   mtor_activation (unscored) +47.9% -> +52.1%  (now fails its own WIDE
                                                  band -- correctly has
                                                  ZERO effect on the
                                                  verdict, see #18, and is
                                                  already labeled
                                                  [FAIL/INFO] rather than
                                                  silently misreported)
   ```
   Overall verdict: still **PASS**. Net effect across every real
   (scored) benchmark point: neutral-to-improved, not a trade-off.
3. **Consolidated the two constants into one** rather than leaving
   `BERGMAN_IVGTT_VG_L_PER_KG` (pathway.py) and `DEFAULT_VG_L_PER_KG`
   (meal.py) as separately-named constants that happen to share a value
   today: `BERGMAN_IVGTT_VG_L_PER_KG = DEFAULT_VG_L_PER_KG` now, so they
   cannot silently drift apart in the future without a deliberate edit.
   Updated `test_ivgtt_vg_uses_literature_anchored_constant` (renamed
   from `..._not_meal_default`, whose whole premise this inverts) to
   assert equality instead of inequality, with a comment explaining why,
   per this document's own established convention for exactly this kind
   of flip (see #17's own test-update note, and the `for_gi()` history
   above).

Full suite: unchanged at 1192 passed, 2 skipped (one test renamed and
rewritten in place, not added). No other test in the suite depended on
the old `0.286` value tightly enough to need updating -- confirmed by
running the full suite, not just the OGTT/IVGTT-specific tests.

### DONE — Fixed `DEFAULT_HEPATIC_EXTRACTION`: was an uncited 0.30, primary literature says 0.10
Follow-up to the entry directly above (Vg): this was left flagged
rather than force-fixed in that earlier pass because a *secondary*-source
read of PMID:651653's numbers seemed methodologically tangled (net
systemic appearance in a tracer study nets against suppressed
endogenous production -- feared it wasn't simply "administered dose
minus extracted dose"). Went back and actually fetched the abstract
live via `PubMedFetcher.fetch_by_pubmed_id('651653')` this pass (still
not full text, but the abstract itself turned out to state the needed
number directly and unambiguously, resolving the earlier worry):

> **Radziuk J, McDonald TJ, Rubenstein D, Dupre J. "Initial splanchnic
> extraction of ingested glucose in normal man." Metabolism.
> 1978;27:657-669. PMID:651653.**
> Nine normal volunteers received a low (45+/-1g) or high (96+/-5g) oral
> glucose load, tracer-labeled separately from IV tracer so oral-origin
> glucose could be distinguished from endogenous production directly
> (not backed out by subtraction) -- exactly the confound the earlier
> pass worried about, and the reason this number IS clean. Of the
> 46+/-3g and 95+/-4g total glucose reaching the systemic pool for each
> dose, 40+/-3g and 86+/-4g respectively originated in the oral load --
> "representing 90% +/-4% of the administered glucose."

Extraction = 1 - 0.90 = **0.10** (SEM range ~0.06-0.14), not the
previous uncited `0.30`. Both tested doses (45g, 96g) bracket this
platform's typical 75g meal and agree to within 1 point (88.9% vs
89.6%), supporting the extrapolation.

`D_eff_mM = carbs_mmol * (1 - hepatic_extraction) / Vg_L` is a pure
amplitude scalar exactly like `Vg_L_per_kg` was (same formula position),
so this changes dose amplitude only, not `Ra(t)`'s timing shape --
confirmed the same way as the Vg fix. Checked the change against
**every** registered clinical benchmark before accepting it (not just
one point), per this session's established practice:

```
                                          before(0.30)   after(0.10)
peak_glucose            [NORMAL, ref 7.8mM]   +5.9%        +17.0%   (both PASS)
glucose_at_120min       [NORMAL, ref 6.5mM]   -4.7%         -0.6%   (both PASS, improved)
peak_insulin            [WIDE,  ref 350pM]    +1.2%        +17.8%   (both PASS)
time_to_peak_insulin    [WIDE,  ref 45min]    -9.1%        -14.5%   (both PASS)
time_to_peak_glucose    [WIDE,  ref 45min]    +9.6%         +8.3%   (both PASS, ~unchanged)
mtor_activation (unscored, no verdict weight) +52.1%       +56.1%
Bergman_IV_glucose (unaffected -- IV route bypasses hepatic extraction entirely)
semaglutide_iauc_5h (WIDE, already-known overshoot gap) +56.4%  +100.8%  (both FAIL/WIDE, doesn't affect verdict)
steroid_t2d_auc_increase [WIDE, ref 50%]      -24.9%       -28.2%   (both PASS)
```

**Verdict on all four datasets is identical before and after: PASS.**
Every currently-passing TIGHT/NORMAL benchmark stays passing; nothing
flips. Being fully honest about the one real cost: the semaglutide
overshoot (already a documented, WIDE-tier, non-verdict-affecting gap,
see the semaglutide entry below) gets meaningfully worse in raw
deviation. Did not treat that as a reason to discard a directly
primary-source-verified number -- per this project's own rule ("never
curve-fit a value to match a benchmark and present it as
literature-derived... document the gap honestly rather than force a
fix"), the gap is now documented as widened, not hidden or used to
justify keeping the uncited guess instead.

Updated the stale test comment in `test_no_hepatic_extraction_applied`
(said "not a 70%-of-that value", now correctly route-agnostic wording
since the fraction itself changed). No test hardcoded the specific
`0.30` value -- all existing `MealInput`/`D_eff_mM` tests are
ratio/relative checks, confirmed by grep before touching anything, so
none needed updating. Full suite: unchanged at 1222 passed, 2 skipped
(constant + 2 comments changed, no tests added or removed).

### DONE — Built the first validation benchmark for a clinically significant drug pathway (semaglutide), corrected an earlier confounded finding
No benchmark existed for ANY drug pathway
    (GLP-1, metformin, cortisol/steroids) before this -- only OGTT/IVGTT
    checked against real data. Found a real, directly comparable trial:
    **Hjerpsted JB, Flint A, Brooks A, Axelsen MB, Kvist T, Blundell J.
    "Semaglutide improves postprandial glucose and lipid metabolism, and
    delays first-hour gastric emptying in subjects with obesity."
    Diabetes Obes Metab. 2018;20(3):610-619. PMID:28941314** (verified
    live via `PubMedFetcher`) -- randomized, double-blind,
    placebo-controlled crossover, n=30, once-weekly 1.0mg semaglutide vs.
    placebo: postprandial glucose incremental AUC (0-5h) reduced by
    **-1.34 mmol.h/L** vs. placebo.

    **An earlier quick check (documented in this file, now corrected) had
    a real confound**: it compared `semaglutide_scenario()` (75g meal,
    the function's own default) against `standard_meal_scenario()` (50g
    meal) as the "placebo," concluding the model undershot the real
    effect (-0.50 vs. -1.34 mmol.h/L, ~37%). Different meal sizes between
    "drug" and "placebo" is not a valid comparison -- a bigger meal alone
    produces a bigger glucose excursion, unrelated to the drug. Building
    the real benchmark surfaced this immediately, because a proper
    benchmark has to construct both arms explicitly with the same inputs.

    **Built properly**: added `ExpertMetrics.glucose_iauc_5h_uM_s` (the
    standard clinical "iAUC(0-5h)" metric -- incremental AUC over a fixed
    5h window, clipped at 0 below baseline, computed in
    `SimulationRunner._compute_expert_metrics()`; 0.0 if the sim ran less
    than 5h) plus a `glucose_iauc_5h_mmol_h_per_L` conversion property
    (the unit real trials report in). Added
    `semaglutide_postprandial_glucose()` (`benchmark.py`) and
    `ModelValidator.validate_semaglutide()` (`validator.py`) -- the
    latter is a genuinely different SHAPE of validation from
    `validate_ogtt()`/`validate_bergman_iv()`: a **comparative** benchmark
    (drug vs. placebo difference), not a single-simulation absolute-value
    check, so it builds two explicit `ScenarioDefinition`s internally
    (same 75g meal, same 5h duration, only the drug event differs) rather
    than reusing library scenario functions with mismatched defaults --
    exactly what the earlier informal check got wrong. Also avoided a
    latent bug in `BenchmarkPoint.check()`: its bounds logic
    (`reference * (1 +/- tolerance_fraction)`) silently produces an
    inverted, always-false range for a negative reference -- never hit
    because every existing benchmark used a positive reference. Sidestepped
    by defining the benchmark's reference as the positive *magnitude* of
    the reduction (1.34) rather than a signed difference, rather than
    touching the shared, already-tested bounds logic for one new caller.

    **Corrected result, properly controlled (same meal size both arms)**:
    model predicts a **2.10 mmol.h/L** reduction vs. the real
    **1.34 mmol.h/L** -- the model actually OVERSHOOTS the real effect
    (+56.4% deviation, WIDE tolerance, fails its own band but -- per
    `_determine_verdict()` -- has no effect on the overall verdict, same
    as `mtor_activation`). This is the opposite conclusion from the
    earlier confounded check, and is the trustworthy one.

    **Not fixed this pass, deliberately**: whether/how to adjust
    `GLP1_MAX_INCRETIN`/`GLP1_EMPTYING_MAX`/`for_semaglutide()`'s
    dose-response coefficients (none of which are individually cited to
    Lau et al. 2015, PMID:26308095 -- that citation covers the
    dose-response *shape*, not these specific magnitudes) is a separate
    decision from building the benchmark that measures them, and doing it
    well means deriving from real receptor-occupancy pharmacology first,
    checking against Hjerpsted second -- not reverse-engineering
    coefficients to hit 1.34 mmol.h/L, which would be exactly the
    curve-fitting-to-a-benchmark anti-pattern this document has
    repeatedly rejected elsewhere (KG_secretion≈200, joint-fit p1≈0.008).
    Added `test_model_does_not_undershoot_the_real_effect` specifically
    to catch a silent reversion to the old, confounded, wrong-direction
    conclusion.

    +7 tests (`TestValidateSemaglutide` x4 in `test_validation.py`;
    3 `ExpertMetrics.glucose_iauc_5h_uM_s` tests in
    `test_simulation_api.py`). Full suite: 1192 -> 1200 passed.

    **Follow-up investigation into "deriving from real receptor-occupancy
    pharmacology first" (above) surfaced a deeper biological-realism
    question, not yet resolved.** Real GLP-1 pharmacology literature (see
    "Clinical Consequences of Delayed Gastric Emptying With GLP-1
    Receptor Agonists and Tirzepatide," J Clin Endocrinol Metab, and
    "Give the Receptor a Brake: Slowing Gastric Emptying by GLP-1,"
    Diabetes 2014) reports that in healthy humans, GLP-1's
    gastric-emptying-slowing effect can *dominate and suppress* net
    postprandial insulin secretion, rather than simply adding to an
    independent amplification effect. `GLP1Pathway`'s current
    architecture treats `incretin_effect` (amplifies secretion) and
    `gastric_emptying_modifier` (slows Ra(t)) as two independent,
    additively-composed signals (rule 11's coupling contract) -- which
    may be too simple if the real physiology has gastric emptying
    delay's downstream effect on glucose-dependent secretion *interacting
    with* (not just running alongside) the direct incretin amplification.
    **Not investigated further this pass** -- this would require reading
    the full quantitative pharmacodynamic literature (a systematic
    review/meta-analysis of gastric emptying delay across GLP-1 agonists,
    plus a rigorous incretin-effect quantification study) carefully
    enough to derive real coefficients, which is a bigger, dedicated
    investigation than fits alongside the semaglutide benchmark work
    above. Documented here as a real, literature-grounded biological-
    realism question -- not a bug, a modeling-architecture question -- so
    a future session doesn't have to rediscover it: is `GLP1Pathway`'s
    two-independent-signals structure still the right one, or does it
    need the two mechanisms to interact?

    **Re-checked (later session, 2026-07-27): neither citation above
    actually supports the claim it's attached to.** Verified both live
    via the real `PubMedFetcher` (not just re-reading this note) --
    PMID:24464721 ("Give the Receptor a Brake," *Diabetes* 2014) returns
    an empty abstract via NCBI efetch: it's a short perspective/
    commentary piece, not a quantitative study, and has no abstract to
    extract dose-response numbers from even in principle. PMID:39418085
    ("Clinical Consequences of Delayed Gastric Emptying With GLP-1RAs and
    Tirzepatide," *J Clin Endocrinol Metab* 2024) has a real abstract,
    but it's about periprocedural GI safety (retained gastric contents at
    endoscopy, aspiration risk, fasting-period guidance) -- not the
    secretion-interaction mechanism this note cites it for at all. So the
    two sources this document has been carrying as the evidence base for
    "gastric-emptying delay may dominate/suppress net insulin secretion
    rather than adding to it" don't actually establish that claim on
    inspection; this looks like the same "cited for a claim its abstract
    doesn't support" pattern this project has caught and corrected for
    other citations before (e.g. the semaglutide-benchmark Nauck 1993
    mismatch). A follow-up search this session (esearch across GLP-1 +
    gastric emptying rate + insulin secretion + quantitative/dose-response
    combinations) did not converge on a clearly on-point quantitative
    source in the time available -- not a confirmed dead end, but not
    resolved either. **Status change**: this is no longer "an
    established finding awaiting quantification" -- it's back to "an
    open modeling-architecture question with an as-yet-unverified
    evidentiary basis." A future session picking this up should start by
    re-deriving the citations from scratch (a systematic review/
    meta-analysis search specifically on quantified gastric-emptying-rate
    vs. insulin-secretion-rate relationships under GLP-1 receptor
    agonism) rather than trusting the two references above.

    **Re-checked again (2026-07-27), still open.** Now that Europe PMC
    full-text fetching exists (see the "Wired Europe PMC full-text
    fetching" entry elsewhere in this file), tried it against this
    file's own three cited GLP-1 physiology PMIDs (8405741, 17098089,
    17928588) plus the liraglutide benchmark's PMID:21340616 -- none
    have open-access full text (`PubMedFetcher(fetch_full_text=True)`
    returns empty for all four), so that specific blocker is confirmed,
    not newly resolved. Ran two further targeted PubMed searches
    (GLP-1 + gastric emptying + insulin secretion + dose-response;
    exendin(9-39) + gastric emptying + insulin secretion + contribution)
    -- neither converged on a paper that directly quantifies the
    gastric-emptying-rate/secretion-rate interaction for exogenous GLP-1
    receptor agonism specifically; results were either unrelated
    supplement/nutrient studies or endogenous-GLP-1 dissection studies
    (post-bariatric-surgery, DPP-4 inhibition, pancreatectomized
    patients) that don't transfer directly to this platform's
    semaglutide/liraglutide dose-response question. Still an open
    question, not a confirmed dead end -- a future session should try
    different search terms (e.g. named drug + "gastric emptying" +
    "insulin secretion" + "mediation" or "structural equation", the
    statistical framing such a dissection study would likely use) rather
    than repeating these two searches.

    **Checked whether the same acute-meal-challenge validation approach
    (that worked for semaglutide) extends to metformin -- not this
    pass, and here's specifically why.** Real acute-metformin
    postprandial literature exists, but the clearest, most directly
    quantified studies found (e.g. Borg et al. 2025, Diabetes Obes Metab,
    examining timing of metformin administration) use **intraduodenal
    glucose infusion with 3-O-methyl-glucose tracer methodology** to
    measure intestinal absorption rate specifically -- a specialized
    research protocol that bypasses gastric emptying entirely and
    measures a different physical quantity than this platform's simple
    oral `MealInput`/`Ra(t)` represents. Building a benchmark against it
    would require either a genuinely comparable standard-oral-meal AUC
    study (not yet found and verified) or introducing new modeling
    machinery to represent intraduodenal delivery, neither of which
    fits this pass. Deliberately did NOT force a comparison against a
    methodologically mismatched study -- that would repeat, in a new
    form, the exact "different conditions labeled placebo vs. drug"
    confound just caught and fixed for semaglutide above. **Next step**:
    find and verify a standard oral-meal-challenge metformin study with
    a directly comparable glucose AUC/iAUC outcome (the same kind of
    study Hjerpsted et al. 2018 was for semaglutide) before attempting a
    `HepGlucPathway`/`for_metformin()` validation benchmark.

    **DONE (later session)**: found and verified Hansen et al. 2024
    (PMID:39049802) -- see the "Built the metformin acute-meal-challenge
    validation benchmark" entry further down this document for the full
    result (model currently undershoots the real effect substantially).

    **Also checked cortisol/steroid pathway for the same acute-benchmark
    opportunity -- found real evidence, but it complicates rather than
    supports a quick benchmark, and raises a genuine biological-realism
    question worth recording precisely.** Searched for an acute-prednisone,
    75g-OGTT, healthy-adult study (the closest population/protocol match
    to this platform's default `steroid_meal()` -- unlike metformin's
    intraduodenal-tracer literature, real OGTT-based prednisone studies
    do exist and use the exact protocol this platform already models).
    Found and live-verified two:
    - **Safety and pharmacodynamic dose response of short-term prednisone
      in healthy adult subjects: a dose ranging, randomized,
      placebo-controlled, crossover study.** PMID:27424036. n=37 healthy
      adults, prednisone 2.5-60mg/day x6-7 days, 75g OGTT on day 6 --
      found NO statistically significant glucose/insulin AUC change vs.
      placebo at ANY dose, including 60mg.
    - **Shah M, Adel MM, Tahsin B, Guerra Y, Fogelfeld L. "Effect of
      short-term prednisone on beta-cell function in subjects with type
      2 diabetes mellitus and healthy subjects." PLoS One. 2020.
      PMID:32369480** (verified live via `PubMedFetcher`). n=5 T2DM + n=5
      healthy adults, prednisone 40mg/day x3 days, 75g OGTT.
      **T2DM group**: glucose AUC increased ~50% (statistically
      significant, p=0.016 vs. healthy). **Healthy group**: glucose AUC
      increased only ~19%, NOT statistically significant. Authors'
      conclusion: reduced beta-cell reserve, not insulin resistance, is
      the primary driver of glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia in T2D
      -- healthy beta cells largely compensate.

    **The real finding, stated carefully**: this is genuine evidence that
    acute/short-term prednisone's glucose-raising effect in HEALTHY
    subjects specifically may be much weaker than `steroid_meal()`'s
    docstring implies ("substantially raises the glucose peak") --
    consistent across two independent studies, one with real statistical
    power (n=37). This does NOT mean the effect is zero or that
    `CortisolPathway` is wrong to model one (T2D patients on steroids are
    a real, important clinical population, and `type2_diabetes_meal_scenario()`
    combined with a `Drug.GLUCOCORTICOID` event would be the population
    where this platform's largest, best-supported effect should show up)
    -- it means the DEFAULT healthy-population `steroid_meal()` scenario's
    framing may overstate what's expected for that specific population.
    **Built the T2D benchmark (the one with real statistical power/
    significance), same session.** Deliberately did NOT attempt the
    healthy-population benchmark -- real evidence says that effect is
    near-null/non-significant, so there's no real number to validate
    against there yet (see "not attempted" note below). Added
    `steroid_t2d_postprandial_glucose()` (`benchmark.py`) and
    `ModelValidator.validate_steroid_meal_t2d()` (`validator.py`) --
    same comparative-benchmark shape as `validate_semaglutide()`: builds
    a T2D-profile `PhysiologicalProfile`, then two explicit
    `ScenarioDefinition`s (same 75g meal, only the `Drug.GLUCOCORTICOID`
    event differs), using the existing `glucose_auc_uM_s` metric (a
    standard OGTT AUC window, not the semaglutide-specific 5h iAUC) to
    compute percent increase vs. the no-steroid arm.

    **Result: a genuine pass.** Model predicts a **37.6%** glucose AUC
    increase vs. the real **50.0%** (Shah et al. 2020's T2D result),
    -24.9% deviation, comfortably within WIDE (50%) tolerance -- not
    forced, not curve-fit to this number (the model's cortisol/hepatic
    coupling was calibrated independently, long before this benchmark
    existed). +5 tests (`TestValidateSteroidMealT2D` in
    `test_validation.py`). Full suite: 1200 -> 1205 passed.

    **Healthy-population benchmark deliberately NOT attempted**: both
    studies found a near-null/non-significant effect in healthy subjects
    (PMID:27424036, PMID:32369480's ~19% non-significant figure) -- there
    is no real, statistically-supported number to validate the model's
    healthy-population steroid effect against yet. Building one now
    would mean picking an arbitrary "expected near-zero" reference
    without a real anchor, the same anti-pattern rejected everywhere
    else in this document. If a future, adequately-powered healthy-
    subject study reports a real, significant effect size, that's the
    point to add this second benchmark -- not before.

    **Checked whether liraglutide (same `GLP1Pathway` mechanism, T2D
    population) gets a third clinical benchmark -- promising real
    evidence found, but NOT built, because the specific number can't be
    primary-source-verified.** A T2D dose-escalation crossover study is
    cited (via a 2015 review, PMC4875959) as finding postprandial
    glucose iAUC(0-5h) 35% lower at 1.2mg and 39% lower at 1.8mg
    liraglutide vs. placebo. Traced the review's reference [61] to its
    actual primary source and verified it live: **Flint A, Kapitza C,
    Hindsberger C, Zdravkovic M. "The once-daily human glucagon-like
    peptide-1 (GLP-1) analog liraglutide improves postprandial glucose
    levels in type 2 diabetes patients." Adv Ther. 2011;28(3):213-26.
    PMID:21340616** (verified live via `PubMedFetcher` -- author names
    confirmed to match exactly; the *review's own reference list* had a
    transcription error, listing different co-author names for the same
    title/journal/year/PMID -- caught by insisting on the live PubMed
    record over the secondary citation, the second time this exact
    failure mode has been caught this session). The paper's own abstract
    (confirmed: n=18 T2D, 3-week crossover, PPG significantly reduced at
    all three doses, p<0.001) does NOT itself state the specific 35%/39%
    percentages -- those are only available via the review's paraphrase.
    No open-access full text exists (Europe PMC: `isOpenAccess=N`,
    subscription-required DOI) to verify the exact figures directly.
    **Not built this pass**: a number available only through a secondary
    source that already had one verified transcription error (the
    author list) is not solid enough ground for a third benchmark,
    following the same discipline applied to the hepatic-extraction and

    primary results table) becomes available, this is otherwise a
    strong, directly comparable candidate (T2D, standard meal challenge,

    exact percentages against the primary text first.

### DONE — Made the GOLD/SILVER/BRONZE confidence-tier CV defaults an explicit, honest assumption, not an unlabeled bare constant
Checked `biosim_uncertainty/distributions.py`'s `LogNormalDistribution
.from_confidence_tier()` for the same "uncited bare constant" pattern
found repeatedly this session (Vg, hepatic extraction, GLP1 constants).
The log-normal *functional form* for kinetic parameters is genuinely
cited (Bar-Even et al. 2011, Nat Chem Biol), but the specific CV values
per tier (GOLD=0.10, SILVER=0.30, BRONZE=0.60) were presented as a plain
default with no citation and no explicit "this is a judgment call"
caveat either -- unlike `HPA_FEEDBACK_GAIN` in `cortisol_pathway.py`,
which already explicitly says "isolated calibration assumption, not
literature-derived."

Researched whether a real citation exists for "typical cross-study CV
of a kinetic parameter measurement" specifically (as opposed to the
log-normal *shape*, which is already covered). Found that the broader
enzyme-kinetics field itself acknowledges this exact quantity is poorly
characterized -- measurement reproducibility studies exist for narrow,
specific comparisons (e.g. ~5% CV when re-fitting the SAME dataset with
different curve-fitting methods) but that measures something different
from cross-STUDY variability, which is what these tiers represent, and
no broadly-applicable single number was found. This is a genuine,
field-wide open problem, not a gap specific to this codebase or
something a citation search could responsibly close.

Fixed by being honest rather than silent: added an explicit note to
both the module docstring and `from_confidence_tier()`'s own docstring
stating these are a documented expert-judgment default (not a directly-
cited statistic), explaining why no more precise citation exists, and
pointing to `HPA_FEEDBACK_GAIN` as the precedent for this same category
of honest, isolated assumption. No numeric or behavioral change --
0.10/0.30/0.60 are unchanged, since there's no better-supported
alternative to replace them with; only the documentation is more
honest. Full suite unchanged at 1205 passed (docs-only change,
`packages/uncertainty` tests re-run to confirm: 46 passed).

### DONE — Genetic uncertainty CV now actually widens Monte Carlo bands (was computed, never wired)
`packages/genotype/src/biosim_genotype/composer.py`'s own module
docstring documents the contract: "The genetic uncertainty CV is
combined in quadrature with the base parameter uncertainty (provided
by the UQ layer in Sprint 5)." `EffectComposer._compose_parameter()`
does correctly compute this per-parameter `ComposedEffect.genetic_cv`,
and `GenotypePersonalizer.personalize()` aggregates it into
`PersonalizationResult.genetic_uncertainty_cv` -- but nothing ever read
either value back out. `runner.py`'s Monte Carlo step built every
UQ distribution via
`LogNormalDistribution.from_confidence_tier(value, "silver")`
unconditionally, genotyped or not, so a `run_uncertainty=True`
simulation for a person carrying e.g. PPARG rs1801282 (which shifts
`p3`'s point estimate ~15%/allele, `effect_db.py`) got a `p3` confidence
band exactly as narrow as the population-average case -- the point
estimate moved but the reported uncertainty around it didn't reflect
that the shift itself came with measurement/effect-size error. Same
"discarded computation" bug class as gi_meals' kabs and the exercise
modifiers (KNOWN BUGS FIXED #15, #16), just at the genotype<->
uncertainty package boundary in `runner.py` rather than inside either
package -- which is why the earlier "audited remaining packages for
computed-but-never-wired" pass (checking each package's own internal
wiring) didn't catch it.

Fixed: `LogNormalDistribution.from_confidence_tier()` gained an
`additional_cv: float = 0.0` parameter, combined with the tier's base
CV in quadrature (`sqrt(tier_cv**2 + additional_cv**2)`); default
preserves prior behaviour exactly. `runner.py` now builds
`genetic_cv_by_param` from `genetic_result.applied_effects` (per-
parameter `ComposedEffect.genetic_cv`, not the already-aggregated
`genetic_uncertainty_cv` -- using the aggregate for every individual
distribution would double-count the same variant's contribution across
all five UQ-tracked parameters) and passes it as `additional_cv` when
constructing each of the five UQ parameter distributions (p1, p2, p3,
ke, EC50_mTOR).

+3 tests in `test_uncertainty.py` (default matches prior behaviour,
quadrature combination is arithmetically correct, additional_cv
strictly widens the distribution). +2 tests in
`test_simulation_api.py`: `test_genetic_variant_widens_the_uq_distribution_for_its_own_parameter`
(patches `LogNormalDistribution.from_confidence_tier` with
`side_effect=<the real classmethod>` so the real computation still
happens, asserts exactly one of the five parameter calls -- p3, from
rs1801282/PPARG -- receives a nonzero `additional_cv`) and
`test_no_genetic_variants_means_zero_additional_cv` (ungenotyped run:
all five calls get `additional_cv=0.0`). Deliberately did NOT assert on
simulated confidence-band width end-to-end: a genetic variant also
shifts the parameter's point estimate, which independently changes
glucose dynamics and confounds a naive "genotyped band is wider"
comparison -- confirmed this by trying exactly that comparison first,
which gave a false failure (genotyped band narrower at the trajectory's
last time point, and only barely wider on the whole-trajectory mean)
purely from that confound, not from the fix being wrong. Verified the
new `test_genetic_variant_widens_...` test fails without the fix
(`git stash` on both changed source files, confirmed `AssertionError`,
restored). Full suite: 1217 -> 1222 passed.

### DONE — `during_exercise_modifiers()["secretion_scale"]` was computed but never wired -- a second, narrower instance of #16
KNOWN BUGS FIXED #16 fixed the exercise personalisation layer's big
"entirely disconnected" gap and, in the same session, closed the
during-vs-after time-gating problem by adding `p1_modifier`/
`extra_g_clearance_modifier` signal slots for `ExercisePathway`. That
fix forwarded `during_exercise_modifiers()["extra_g_clearance"]` but
missed the same dict's other key, `["secretion_scale"]`
(catecholamine-mediated suppression of insulin secretion during acute
exercise) -- `ExercisePathway.output_signals()` only ever read
`during["extra_g_clearance"]`, and `GlucoseInsulinPathway.dydt()`'s
signal contract (rule 11) had no slot for it even if it had been
forwarded. Same "computed but discarded" bug class as gi_meals' kabs
and the post-exercise modifiers themselves -- just a second instance
inside the same module that #16 didn't fully close, this time the
in-progress-bout suppression rather than the post-bout sensitisation.
Test coverage had the identical blind spot: the existing test asserted
`during_exercise_modifiers()["secretion_scale"] < 1.0` directly on the
bare dict, never through the actual pathway or a simulation.

Fixed: added a ninth coupling-contract signal,
`secretion_scale_modifier` (rule 11, mult. on `secretion_scale`,
neutral default 1.0), consumed in `GlucoseInsulinPathway.dydt()`
exactly like `p1_modifier`/`extra_g_clearance_modifier` were --
`secretion_scale_eff = p.secretion_scale * s.get("secretion_scale_modifier", 1.0)`,
used in place of the bare `p.secretion_scale` for both
`delta_secretion` and `first_phase_secretion`. Both terms are already
zero at the analytic basal steady state by construction (gated on
`current_frac == basal_frac` and `dG <= 0` respectively), so this
preserves basal invariance regardless of the modifier's value -- no
different from how `p3_modifier`/`gb_modifier` already work. Wired
`ExercisePathway.output_signals()` to forward
`during["secretion_scale"]` while the bout is in progress and `1.0`
after it ends (post-exercise sensitisation genuinely doesn't include
this acute suppression -- confirmed `post_exercise_modifiers()` has no
such key), added the new signal to `exercise_couplings()`'s forwarded
list and `PathwayDescriptor.output_signals`.

+4 tests: two at the `dydt()` level mirroring the existing
`p1_modifier`/`p3_modifier` pattern (basal-invariance, and suppresses
secretion away from basal), one locking `exercise_couplings()`'s exact
five-signal set (so a future new signal can't repeat this exact
drift), and one full end-to-end simulation test
(`test_secretion_scale_modifier_wired_through_to_gi`) that
reconstructs the pre-fix behaviour by patching
`ExercisePathway.output_signals()` to strip the key, confirming peak
insulin during a meal eaten mid-bout is measurably lower with the
wiring present than without it. Verified the two regression tests
(the wiring test and the away-from-basal unit test) both fail without

### DONE — `biosim_lay.FOOD_DB`'s qualitative `gi_category` had drifted out of sync with the numeric GI actually used for absorption-rate math, mislabeling 5 foods
Same "same fact duplicated across two files/packages, no cross-check"
bug shape already caught this session for `Vg_L_per_kg` and
`MODEL_VERSION` -- this time on categorical food data rather than a
scalar constant. `biosim_lay/food_items.py`'s `FOOD_DB` hardcodes a
`gi_category` string per food ("high"/"medium"/"low"/"negligible", per
the field's own documented thresholds: high>70, medium 55-70, low<55).
`biosim_seeds/gi_meals.py`'s `GI_VALUES` maintains an independent,
Atkinson et al. 2008 (PMID:18835944)-sourced numeric GI for the same
foods, actually used by `gi_adjusted_kabs()` for real absorption-rate
math (see KNOWN BUGS FIXED-adjacent `test_gi_meal_scenario_carries_computed_kabs`
fix). Nothing ever checked the two against each other. Checking by
hand against the field's own stated rule found 5 real mismatches, not
just a rounding-boundary quibble:

```
food_id              numeric GI   correct category   was labeled
cola_330ml               63.0        medium              high
orange_juice_200ml       50.0        low                 high    <- worst: opposite category
banana_medium             51.0        low                 medium
wholegrain_bread          53.0        low                 medium
grapes_100g               46.0        low                 medium
```

Impact: `foods_by_gi_category()` is `biosim_lay`'s public, exported
function -- the natural one a "choose lower-GI foods" lay-guidance
feature would call. A user asking for low-GI swaps would never see
orange juice even though the platform's own simulation-driving numeric
data says it qualifies -- guidance opposite to what the model itself
implies.

Fixed the 5 literals to match `GI_VALUES` (the number with a real
citation and actual downstream use, treated as ground truth). Rather
than leaving this as a one-time literal fix that could drift again,
added `gi_category_for_value(gi: float) -> str` to `food_items.py` --
a canonical implementation of the field's own documented threshold
rule -- and a cross-package regression test,
`test_food_db_categories_match_gi_values_numeric_ground_truth` in
`packages/data-seeds/tests/test_gi_meals.py`, checking every food
present in both tables. Deliberately placed in `data-seeds`, not
`lay-output`: `data-seeds` already depends on `lay-output`
(`gi_meals.py`'s own `from biosim_lay.food_items import FOOD_DB`), so
adding the reverse dependency just to share one table would invert an
existing, working architecture for a data-consistency check that fits
just as well as a test. (Noted but did not touch: `GIFoodItem
.gi_category` in `gi_meals.py` is a *third*, independently-written
implementation of this same categorisation, using `>=70` for high
instead of `food_items.py`'s documented `>70` -- doesn't change the
outcome for any current food since none sit at exactly GI=70, so left
alone rather than risk an unrelated behavioural change to already-passing,
already-tested code.)

+1 test. Verified it fails without the fix (`git stash` on
