a distinct check from bandit (which analyzes this project's own source,
not the packages it depends on). Result: no known vulnerabilities in any
pinned dependency. A clean result, not a gap -- recorded here so this
specific check isn't re-run from scratch believing it was never done.
Added to `requirements.txt` alongside `bandit`/`ruff`/`pytest-cov`.

### DONE (spot-checked, not adopted as a gate) — First mypy run, findings are type-strictness noise, not bugs
Ran `mypy packages --ignore-missing-imports` for the first time this
session: 48 errors across 13 files. Unlike the ruff pass above (which
specifically flags *unreachable/discarded* code -- a strong bug signal,
and found two real ones), mypy here flags *type-unprovable* code, which
is a much weaker signal on a codebase that has never been written
mypy-strict and is instead verified by 1187 passing tests. Spot-checked
the highest-signal-looking findings rather than triaging all 48:

- `coupling.py`'s `CompositePathway.with_meals()`: mypy flags
  `p.with_meals(meals)` since `with_meals` isn't defined on the abstract
  `BasePathway` type of `p`. Checked the surrounding code: it's a
  deliberate `hasattr(p, "with_meals")`-guarded duck-typing pattern (the
  list is pre-filtered to `meal_capable` before the call) -- mypy can't
  verify `hasattr` guards without a `TypeGuard`, so this is a known
  static-analysis limitation, not a reachable `AttributeError`.
- `types.py`'s `ParameterValue.uncertainty_range`: mypy flags
  `self.uncertainty_upper - self.uncertainty_lower` since both are
  `Optional[float]`. Checked: it's guarded by `if self.has_uncertainty`
  immediately above, which itself checks both are not `None` -- mypy
  can't narrow `Optional` across a separate property call, so this is
  also a real guard mypy can't see, not an unguarded subtraction.
- The large cluster of `"object" has no attribute ...` errors across
  `runner.py`/`library.py`/`batch.py` all trace to one deliberate typing
  choice: `PersonalizationSpec.physiological_profile: Optional[object]`
  in `scenario.py` (loosely typed to avoid a circular import between
  `simulation-api` and `physiology`). Everything downstream that reads
  `.body_weight_kg`/`.disease_states`/etc. off it inherits the same
  `object` type mypy can't resolve further -- one root cause, not dozens
  of independent bugs.

**Not adopted as a CI gate and not mass-refactored.** Getting this
codebase to a clean mypy run would need real, deliberate investment
(`Protocol` classes for the duck-typed pathway interfaces, resolving the
`physiological_profile: object` shortcut properly) -- a substantial,
cross-cutting typing pass, not a quick fix, and none of the findings
spot-checked here point to an actual runtime defect the way the ruff
F841 sweep's two real bugs did. Documented so a future session
understands *why* mypy is noisy here rather than re-discovering the same
three root causes from scratch, and doesn't mistake "never run" for
"never investigated."

### DONE — IDRegistry.register()'s collision check made the documented entity-merge workflow entirely non-functional
`deprecated_canonical_ids` is `IDRegistry.register()`'s documented
mechanism for merging two entities that legitimately share a real-world
identifier (e.g. two curated records for the same metabolite that turn
out to be the same HMDB accession). But the cross-reference collision
check raised `ValueError` unconditionally whenever ANY existing entity
already owned that accession, with no exemption for the case where that
existing entity is being deprecated BY THE SAME CALL -- the one case
`deprecated_canonical_ids` exists to support. Since `register()` is the
only method that adds data (no separate `update()`/`merge()` exists),
this made the merge workflow completely unreachable: every attempt to
merge two entities sharing a cross-reference raised the same collision
error as a genuine, unrelated duplicate-registration bug, with no way to
distinguish the two from the caller's side.

A second, latent bug sat behind the first: even bypassing the check
directly (e.g. patching around it to test), nothing removed the
deprecated entity's OLD entry from `_xref_index` for that accession, so
`resolve()` would then see TWO owners and raise `AmbiguousResolutionError`
for what should now be an unambiguous, correctly-merged lookup.

Fixed both in `register()`: the collision check now computes
`deprecated_strs = {str(old_id) for old_id in deprecated}` and only
raises when `non_deprecated_owners` (existing owners of the accession
NOT in that set) is non-empty; the xref-index-building step now rebuilds
each key's owner list with any deprecated-and-superseded entries removed
before appending the new canonical ID, so the merged entity becomes the
accession's sole owner. A genuine third-party collision (no shared
deprecation) still raises exactly as before -- verified directly, not
just asserted.

+3 tests in `test_resolver.py::TestDeprecation`: one confirms the merge
call itself no longer raises, one confirms `resolve()` returns the new
canonical ID unambiguously afterward, one confirms an unrelated
accession collision during a merge attempt still correctly raises.
Verified both merge-path tests fail without the fix (via `git stash` on
`registry.py`) and pass with it; the third-party-collision test passes
in both states, confirming the fix is a precise exemption, not a
blanket bypass. Full suite: 1282 -> 1285 passed, 2 skipped (unchanged).

### DONE — CurationQueue.enqueue_conflict()'s conflict_id was order-dependent, defeating its own dedup
`conflict_id = f"conflict:{parameter_id_a}:{parameter_id_b}"` had no
canonicalization: reporting the identical parameter conflict with the
two parameter IDs swapped (e.g. a re-scan of the same paper pair that
happens to iterate in the other order) produced a DIFFERENT item_id,
silently bypassing `enqueue()`'s "already in queue, bump priority
instead of duplicating" dedup logic entirely -- the same real-world
conflict would be enqueued twice as two independent curation items.
Found while investigating the id-resolver merge-workflow bug above
(same investigation surfaced both); deferred until now since it has
zero current production callers, unlike id-resolver which blocked an
entire documented feature outright.

Fixed by canonicalizing the two parameter IDs with `sorted()` before
building the key, so either call order maps to the same `conflict_id`.
Deliberately minimal: only the id-construction step changes -- which
value/source is `_a` vs `_b` in the resulting item's reason text is
untouched, since that ordering is caller-supplied context, not part of
the identity of "which two parameters conflict."

+1 test: enqueues the same conflict twice with the parameter IDs (and
their associated values/sources) swapped, asserts both calls return the
same `item_id` and only one item ends up pending. Verified it fails
without the fix (`conflict:p1:p2` != `conflict:p2:p1`) and passes with
it. Full suite: 1285 -> 1286 passed, 2 skipped (unchanged).

### DONE — BatchRunner.run_all() swallowed the actual exception behind a batch failure
`except Exception as e: failed.append(name)` discarded `str(e)`
entirely -- a scenario name appearing in `BatchResult.failed_names` gave
no way to tell a real, systemic bug (e.g. every scenario in a sweep
failing the same way) from an unrelated, expected one-off failure,
mirroring the exact bug class already fixed in `PopulationRunner`
(see the bandit B110 entry above) but never carried over to
`BatchRunner`, its parallel-execution sibling. Flagged during the same
investigation as the two fixes above, deferred as lower-priority than
both since it's a debuggability gap, not a functional block.

Fixed the same way: added `BatchResult.failure_reasons: list[str]`,
populated with `f"{name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"` per failure inside
`run_all()`'s except clause.

+1 test (`test_failure_reason_is_recorded_not_swallowed`), monkeypatching
`SimulationRunner.run` to force a known `ValueError` across a batch and
asserting `failure_reasons` captures it, following the identical pattern
`test_population.py::TestPopulationRunnerFailureHandling` already
established. Verified it fails without the fix (`AttributeError:
'BatchResult' object has no attribute 'failure_reasons'`) and passes
with it. Full suite: 1286 -> 1287 passed, 2 skipped (unchanged).

### DONE — GLP1Parameters.dpp4_inhibited()'s glp1_peak field was a pure no-op, and its test only ever checked the dead field
`GLP1Parameters.dpp4_inhibited()` set `glp1_peak=GLP1_PEAK_PM * 1.8`,
clearly intended to model DPP-4 inhibitors directly raising postprandial
GLP-1 peak concentration. But `glp1_peak` was never read by `dydt()` or
`output_signals()` -- the ONLY consumer anywhere in the codebase was
`test_glp1.py::test_dpp4_inhibited_raises_peak`, which asserted
`dpp4.glp1_peak > default.glp1_peak` on the bare dataclass, never
through a simulation. Same "discarded computation, only asserted on the
params object" blind spot the ruff F841 sweep entry above already
caught twice (gi_meals kabs, caffeine_and_meal_scenario) -- this is a
third instance ruff didn't flag itself (the assignment IS read, just
only by a test that couldn't tell the difference).

Verified empirically before touching anything: ran a 75g-meal simulation
through `couple_with_gi()` with `dpp4_inhibited()`'s real params vs. an
identical copy with `glp1_peak` reset to default -- max abs difference
across every species, 0.0. The entire modeled DPP-4-inhibitor effect
comes solely from the half-life doubling.

Checked whether `glp1_peak` should instead be wired in rather than
removed: the file's own docstring cites Deacon 2011 (PMID:21114598) for
the DPP-4 mechanism, but the live-fetched abstract (verified via
`PubMedFetcher.fetch_by_pubmed_id`) is a general antidiabetic-efficacy
review with no specific GLP-1 fold-elevation figure -- no primary source
anchors a specific peak-elevation magnitude. Per this session's standing
rule against curve-fitting an unanchored number to look plausible,
removed the dead field entirely (`GLP1Parameters.__init__`,
`GLP1_PEAK_PM` module constant, and the `dpp4_inhibited()` assignment)
rather than inventing a formula for it.

Replaced the blind-spot test with
`test_dpp4_inhibited_raises_simulated_glp1_peak`, which runs both a
baseline and a `dpp4_inhibited()` composite through `ODESystem` with a
real meal and asserts the actual simulated GLP1 trajectory's peak is
higher under DPP-4 inhibition -- checking the one mechanism (half-life)
that is genuinely wired in, instead of a field that never was. Note:
unlike this session's other fixes, this test doesn't discriminate
old-vs-new code (the half-life effect was already correctly wired
before this fix) -- its value is closing the blind spot going forward,
not retroactively catching the removed field, which was already proven
inert directly (see above) rather than via pytest. Full suite unchanged
at 1287 passed, 2 skipped (one test replaced, not added).

**Separately found while investigating, not fixed (deferred)**: the
same experiment revealed `GLP1_MEAL_RESPONSE` (0.035 pM per mM glucose
above `ec50_secretion`) produces a postprandial GLP1 peak only ~1.05x
basal for a 75g high-sugar meal -- far below this same file's own
docstring, which documents basal GLP-1 as ~5-15 pM and postprandial peak
as ~30-80 pM (a 3-6x rise). Existing tests never caught this because
they only ever assert relative comparisons (semaglutide peak lower than
baseline peak, etc.), never an absolute value against the literature
range stated in the file's own docstring. Properly anchoring
`GLP1_MEAL_RESPONSE` needs a literature-sourced dose-response curve
(candidate: Nauck et al. 1993, PMID:8405741, already cited in this
file), not a guessed multiplier -- the same category of "needs a real
literature-anchoring pass, not a quick fix" as the already-deferred
GLP1 gastric-emptying/incretin architecture question. Left for a future
milestone.

**Re-checked immediately after** (same session): live-fetched all three
of this file's cited PMIDs via `PubMedFetcher` looking for a usable
basal/peak concentration figure to anchor `GLP1_MEAL_RESPONSE` --
8405741 (Nauck 1993) is actually an *exogenous GLP-1 infusion* study in
poorly-controlled T2D patients (normalizing fasting glucose), not an
endogenous postprandial secretion measurement, so it doesn't even
support the physiological claim it's cited for; 17098089 and 17928588
are general incretin-system/physiology reviews whose 250-word abstracts
don't carry the specific pM figures either. Confirmed genuinely blocked
on abstract-only literature access, same as the liraglutide benchmark --
not attempted further.

### DONE — SimulationRunner's drug-only "quick path" computed personalized params correctly but never recorded them
`run()` has two branches that call `PhysiologicalPersonalizer().personalize()`:
a "quick path" (lines ~100-108, taken whenever `personalization
.physiological_profile` is `None` but drug events or an `exercise_bout`
exist) and the main, profile-driven path (lines ~109-128). Both compute
a real `PhysiologicalPersonalizationResult` and both correctly used it
to update the ODE simulation's own `params` -- the simulated numbers
were never wrong. But only the main path assigned the result to
`physio_result`; the quick path discarded its own `r2` return value
entirely, so `SimulationOutput.physiological_personalization` stayed
`None` even though real personalization had genuinely been applied.

Not a rare edge case: `biosim_rest.service.scenario_in_to_definition()`
never sets `personalization` on the scenarios it builds, so **every REST
`/simulate` request that includes `drug_events`** takes exactly this
path. Confirmed a concrete downstream consequence in
`biosim_infra.infra.create_bundle()`, which falls back to unmodified
default `PathwayParameters()` whenever `physiological_personalization`
is `None`: ran a metformin (2000mg, chronic) scenario with no profile
through both `SimulationRunner` and `create_bundle()` -- the actual
simulation used personalized `p3=1.156e-06, Gb=4.8, p1=0.0349`, but the
bundle's recorded `parameter_values` were the unmodified defaults
(`p3=9.032e-07, Gb=5.0, p1=0.0317`). A `ReproducibilityBundle` for any
drug-only REST scenario was silently recording the wrong parameters,
defeating its purpose.

Fixed with a one-line addition (`physio_result=r2`) in the quick-path
branch, mirroring the main branch. The existing downstream block that
re-syncs `physio_result.personalized_params` after the glucocorticoid
secretion_scale adjustment (lines 139-144) already handles both branches
uniformly once `physio_result` is actually set.

+1 test (`test_drug_only_quick_path_still_records_physiological_personalization`):
runs a metformin-only, no-profile scenario (the quick path) and asserts
`physiological_personalization` is not `None` and its recorded `Gb` is
genuinely lowered (not the unmodified default). Verified it fails
without the fix (`AssertionError: assert None is not None`) and passes
with it. Full suite: 1287 -> 1288 passed, 2 skipped (unchanged).

### DONE — `SimulationCache._key()` collided across scenarios that differ only in personalization, drug timing, or meal GI
Surfaced as a hypothesis by a background codebase-read pass (not trusted
until independently reproduced -- see this file's evidence-hierarchy
policy), then verified directly: `ScenarioDefinition.to_dict()`
(`scenario.py`) omitted `personalization` **entirely**, plus
`MealEvent.glycaemic_index`/`kabs`, `DrugEvent.hours_before_simulation`,
and `exercise_bout_in_progress`. `SimulationCache._key()`
(`biosim_infra/infra.py`) hashes `json.dumps(scenario.to_dict())`
verbatim, so any two scenarios sharing a name/duration/meals(minus
GI/kabs)/drugs(minus timing) but differing only in one of those omitted
fields produced a byte-identical SHA-256 key.

Reproduced directly before touching anything: a healthy scenario and an
otherwise-identical Type-2-diabetes-personalized scenario (same name,
same single meal) hashed to the exact same key. Same confirmed for a
GI=100 vs. GI=30 meal, and for a caffeine-now vs. caffeine-3h-ago drug
event. This is live today through the REST API specifically for drug
timing (`DrugEventIn.hours_before_simulation` is wire-exposed and passed
through by `scenario_in_to_definition()`); the GI/personalization
collisions are reachable today via internal callers (`biosim_seeds`)
and would become REST-live the moment those fields are added to
`ScenarioIn`, which is plausible near-term work -- fixed now rather than
left as a landmine.

**Fix, with one deliberate privacy constraint -- caught and corrected by
the mandatory security-reviewer pass, not right on the first attempt**:
`to_dict()` now includes all of the above. `personalization
.genetic_variants` is the one field that could carry raw rsIDs
(`Variant.rsid`) -- since `to_dict()` is documented as usable "for
archiving and API transport" (i.e. not guaranteed to stay
purely-internal-hash-input forever), rule 7 (no raw rsIDs in anything
that could be exported) applies defensively even though today's only
real consumer is the cache key.

First attempt represented genetic variants as a bare `sha256(rsid
:genotype)[:16]` fingerprint. The mandatory security-reviewer pass (run
per this project's own rule for anything touching physiology/genetic
personalization) correctly flagged this as CRITICAL, not adequate: `rsid`
is drawn from a small, publicly cataloged space, and this platform's own
`VariantEffectDB` has only ~14 known SNPs x 3 `Genotype` values = <=42
real combinations -- an unkeyed hash of that is an exhaustive lookup
table, not a one-way function. Truncation length was a red herring;
a full untruncated SHA-256 would have been equally reversible. Verified
this finding myself before accepting it (didn't just trust the agent's
claim): confirmed the exact SNP count directly against `effect_db.py`'s
`default()` (7 SNPs) and `extended_t2d_variants()` (7 more unique).

Fixed by keying the hash: `hmac.new(_FINGERPRINT_KEY, ...)` where
`_FINGERPRINT_KEY` is generated via `secrets.token_bytes(32)` once at
process start and never persisted/exported/read from config -- closes
the brute-force path (the attacker no longer knows the key) at zero
new operational cost (no secret to manage, satisfies "no paid API keys"
and this project's existing secret-management rules). Trade-off,
documented directly in `_variant_fingerprint()`'s docstring: this makes
the fingerprint process-local, not a stable cross-process identifier --
fine for `SimulationCache` (already in-memory/per-process), but a future
implementer wiring `ReproducibilityBundle` to actually use `to_dict()`
must not reuse this fingerprint scheme for that (see the gap noted
below) and needs to re-derive from the original `Variant` input instead.

Confirmed `ReproducibilityBundle.create_bundle()` doesn't currently even
call `scenario.to_dict()` (it hand-builds `scenario_dict` from just
name/description -- a separate, real reproducibility gap, noted but not
fixed here since it's outside this bug's scope), so there was no live
export path to double-check against; the keyed-fingerprint design is a
defensive choice for `to_dict()`'s documented future use, not a reaction
to an existing leak.

**Second round, also caught by mandatory code review, also not right on
the first attempt**: the code-reviewer agent found that
`_variant_fingerprint()` hashed only `rsid:genotype.value`, but
`EffectComposer.compose()` actually calls
`variant.dosage_for_allele(risk_allele)`, which reads
`observed_alleles`/`ref_allele`/`alt_allele` FIRST and only falls back to
genotype alone when none of those are set. Two homozygous calls for the
same SNP with opposite observed letters -- e.g. protective "CC" vs. risk
"TT" for rs7903146, both `Genotype.HOMOZYGOUS_ALT` -- have identical
rsid+genotype but opposite `dosage_for_allele()` results (0 vs. 2): the
exact same "23andMe homozygous call" bug class already fixed elsewhere
in this file (KNOWN BUGS FIXED, "Homozygous 23andMe/two-letter genotype
calls silently reported the WRONG dosage"), reintroduced by this PR's own
attempt to fix a different collision. Verified myself before accepting
(checked `dosage_for_allele()`'s actual priority order in
`variant.py` and `EffectComposer.compose()`'s actual field usage in
`composer.py`, then reproduced the exact collision through
`cache.get()`/`cache.put()`) rather than trusting the agent's claim
outright. Fixed by including `observed_alleles`/`ref_allele`/`alt_allele`
in the fingerprint input alongside rsid+genotype. Confirmed
`chromosome`/`position` do NOT need to be included -- `EffectComposer
.compose()` only ever reads `variant.rsid` and
`variant.dosage_for_allele()`, so those two fields are pure provenance
metadata that can't affect the simulated output. The code-reviewer's
second finding (fingerprint reversibility) described the pre-HMAC
bare-hash version reviewed in parallel with the security-reviewer pass
above; already resolved by the keyed-HMAC fix, not a separate action.

+7 tests total in `test_infrastructure.py` (`TestSimulationCache`):
different-drug-timing, different-GI, different-personalization,
different-genetic-variant-present, and different-observed-alleles
(same rsid+genotype, opposite letters) all assert a previously-colliding
pair now misses the cache; a seventh asserts no raw rsid string ever
appears in `json.dumps(scenario.to_dict())`. Verified RED first: stashed
only the `scenario.py` fix via `git stash` for the first three
collision tests (confirmed each failed by returning the other
scenario's cached `SimulationOutput`, not just a `_key()` string
mismatch); for the observed-alleles case, temporarily narrowed
`_variant_fingerprint()`'s input back to `rsid:genotype` only, confirmed
that specific test failed the same way, then restored the full fix --
GREEN throughout. Full suite: 1288 -> 1294 passed, 2 skipped
(unchanged). `KNOWN_TEST_COUNT` in `app.py` updated to 1294.

**Not fixed this pass, noted for a future milestone**: the
`ReproducibilityBundle`/`create_bundle()` gap above (`scenario_dict`
doesn't actually capture meals/drugs/personalization despite the field
comment implying it uses `to_dict()`) -- a real, separate
reproducibility bug, out of scope for a caching-correctness fix.

`@property def has_disease(self, state: DiseaseState = DiseaseState.HEALTHY)`
-- a property getter can't accept caller-supplied arguments, so

`state in profile.disease_states` checks (`runner.py:435`,
`modifiers.py`), and `is_diabetic`/`is_insulin_resistant` cover the

Full suite unchanged at 1294 passed, 2 skipped (pure deletion, no
replacement behavior needed).

### DONE — `PlatformSession.simulate()` built a literature-loaded pathway, then silently discarded it and ran hardcoded defaults instead
Surfaced as a hypothesis by the same background codebase-read pass as
the cache-collision bug above; personally verified before touching
anything, same as that fix. `simulate()`'s no-profile branch built a
`GlucoseInsulinPathway`/`ODESystem` from `self._base_params` (the
literature-loaded parameters `PlatformSession.__init__` documents
loading by default via `use_literature_params=True`), then discarded
both and ran the scenario through a bare `SimulationRunner()` instead --
which itself hardcoded a fresh `PathwayParameters()` inside `run()`. The
personalised branch had the identical gap (also just called
`SimulationRunner()` with no base params passed). Net effect:
`use_literature_params` (the class's headline, default-on constructor
argument) had **zero effect on `simulate()`'s actual simulated output**
-- only `export_sbml()` ever used `self._base_params`.

Confirmed directly, not assumed: `session.base_params ==
PathwayParameters()` byte-for-byte today, which is *why* this was
invisible -- the seeded literature values currently happen to equal the
hardcoded class defaults exactly. That's a coincidence of today's
`ParameterStore` snapshot, not a structural guarantee (rule 5: the store
is append-only and meant to evolve), so this was a real, latent
landmine: the moment a literature-curated value diverges from the class
default, every `PlatformSession` simulation would silently keep using
the wrong (unpersonalized-by-literature) parameters.

Fix: added an optional `base_params: Optional[PathwayParameters] = None`
to `SimulationRunner.__init__`, used in place of the bare
`PathwayParameters()` at the top of `run()` (defaults to
`PathwayParameters()` when omitted, so every other existing caller of
`SimulationRunner()` -- REST API, `CachedRunner`, batch/population
tooling, comparison reports -- is unaffected). `PlatformSession
.simulate()` now passes `SimulationRunner(base_params=self._base_params)`
in one unified return, replacing the old two-branch logic entirely (no
more pathway/system built only to be thrown away). Manually traced
`run()`'s full downstream flow to confirm this doesn't get bypassed
anywhere: physiological personalisation, the glucocorticoid
secretion_scale adjustment, and genetic personalisation all correctly
reassign the same local `params` variable (via `dataclasses.replace()` /
`.personalized_params`, never in-place mutation), which is what
ultimately feeds `GlucoseInsulinPathway`. Also confirmed empirically
(not just by code reading) that `self._base_params` is never mutated
across repeated `simulate()` calls on the same session -- deep-copied it
before three consecutive calls (including one with a T2D profile) and
diffed after: unchanged.

+2 tests: `test_base_params_override_changes_output`
(`test_simulation_api.py`, `SimulationRunner(base_params=PathwayParameters
(Gb=6.5))` vs. default, asserts the fasted glucose baseline actually
differs) and `test_simulate_actually_uses_base_params`
(`test_session.py`, reaches into `PlatformSession._base_params` directly
to prove the wiring, since today's real literature values can't
demonstrate it through the public `use_literature_params` flag alone).
Both RED-proofed via `git stash` on just the respective source file
before restoring the fix. Full suite: 1294 -> 1296 passed, 2 skipped.

**Review-process note**: the mandatory code-reviewer and
security-reviewer passes for this fix both failed on launch --
"session limit, resets 6:30am (Europe/London)" -- a quota outage, not a
finding. Rather than block on a resource that was going to fail
identically on retry, did the equivalent verification personally and
directly instead (the questions I would have asked the agents: does
`self._base_params` survive every downstream branch of `run()` without
being bypassed; is there any in-place-mutation risk to the now-shared,
reused `_base_params` object; did removing the discarded
pathway/system construction lose any side effect from those
constructors) -- documented above with the actual evidence for each,
same standard this file already holds agent-assisted findings to.

### DONE — `PlatformSession` built its cache runner via a fragile `__new__` bypass; separately, its caching is entirely inert
Found while investigating the same background-read report as the two
entries above. Two related but distinct issues:

1. **Fixed**: `PlatformSession.__init__` built `self._cached_runner` via
   `CachedRunner.__new__(CachedRunner)` plus a manual `self._cached_runner
   ._cache = SimulationCache(...)` assignment, bypassing `CachedRunner
   .__init__()` entirely for no reason -- `CachedRunner.__init__` already
   accepts an optional `cache` param built for exactly this. Replaced
   with a plain `CachedRunner(cache=SimulationCache(max_size=cache_size))`
   call. No behavior change (verified: full suite unchanged at 1296
   passed), purely removes a fragile pattern that would silently skip any
   future `CachedRunner.__init__` setup logic.
2. **Not fixed this pass, next milestone**: while checking this,
   confirmed `PlatformSession.simulate()` never actually calls
   `self._cached_runner.run(...)` at all -- both branches always
   construct a fresh `SimulationRunner` directly (now with `base_params`
   correctly threaded through, per the entry above, but still bypassing
   the cache). Confirmed empirically: three consecutive identical
   `session.simulate("fasted")` calls leave `cache_stats()` at
   `hits=0, misses=0, size=0`. `PlatformSession`'s advertised caching
   (`cache_size` constructor arg, `self._cached_runner`, `cache_stats()`)
   is real, correctly built, and entirely unused for its actual purpose
   -- the same "computed but never wired" bug class as several entries
   above, just not yet fixed. This is a performance/architectural gap,

This was the highest-value remaining item per this file's own stated

verified via the actual `biosim_literature.fetcher.PubMedFetcher
.fetch_by_pubmed_id()` class (not just esearch), reading the raw XML
directly rather than trusting a console-rendered copy (the `×` in

the raw response). Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind
crossover, n=15 T2D (median HbA1c 50 mmol/mol [6.7%], BMI 30.1, age 71):

by **MD 186 mmol/L·min [95% CI 64-307]** (saline/non-GLP-1R-blocked arm
-- the correct comparator, since this platform doesn't model exendin
(9-39) antagonism). Metformin dose (1000-2000mg/day, titrated) confirmed
via ClinicalTrials.gov's public API for NCT03246451 (the abstract didn't
state it) -- a legitimate primary-source cross-check, not a guess.

(same shape as the existing `glucose_iauc_5h_uM_s`/`_mmol_h_per_L`, just
a 4h window instead of 5h -- a separate field, not a parameterized

5h metric returns 0.0 for anything under 5h, and reusing it by simply
running a 5h scenario instead of the trial's actual 4h protocol would
have been exactly the "different conditions labeled placebo vs. drug"
confound this file has already caught and rejected once (semaglutide's
first, wrong-conclusion attempt).

(`benchmark.py`) and `ModelValidator.validate_metformin()`

(this platform's standard reference meal size; the paper's abstract
didn't state exact meal composition), 4h duration, WIDE tolerance.
Wired into `validate_all()`.

**undershoots substantially** -- predicts a **20.66 mmol.min/L**

### DONE — `PlatformSession.simulate()` now actually routes through its own cache (follow-on to the `CachedRunner.__new__` entry above)
Closed the gap that entry deliberately deferred: `CachedRunner.__init__`
now accepts the same `base_params` override `SimulationRunner.__init__`
got earlier this session, used in place of a bare `SimulationRunner()`
inside `CachedRunner.run()`. `PlatformSession.simulate()` now calls
`self._cached_runner.run(scenario)` instead of constructing a fresh
`SimulationRunner` directly for every call -- the branch that used to
bypass the cache is gone.

**Only safe now because of the `SimulationCache._key()` collision fix
earlier this session** -- before that fix, wiring a
personalization-bearing `simulate()` call through the cache would have
risked serving one scenario's result for a genuinely different one
(different disease state, drug timing, etc., all previously ignored by
`to_dict()`). That's plausibly the real reason this was never connected
in the first place: caching was correctly built, but connecting it
safely required a fix that hadn't happened yet. Worth remembering as a
concrete example of why this session's milestones ended up in the order
they did, not an arbitrary one.

**One real snag caught by a test that already existed from an earlier
milestone**, not a fresh agent finding: `CachedRunner` captures
`base_params` once at construction, but the earlier milestone's own
`test_simulate_actually_uses_base_params` deliberately reassigns
`session._base_params` *after* construction to prove wiring (see that
test's own comment). That mutation stopped propagating to
`self._cached_runner`'s independent copy the moment caching was wired
in -- caught immediately by running the full `test_session.py` file
before committing, not discovered later. Fixed by syncing
`self._cached_runner._base_params = self._base_params` right before
each `run()` call in `simulate()`, rather than only at `__init__` time --
cheap, and correct regardless of whether `_base_params` is ever
reassigned post-construction.

Strengthened rather than just added to: the pre-existing
`test_cache_stats` test asserted only `"hit_rate" in stats` -- true
before, during, and after this entire bug existed, so it silently never
caught that caching was inert. Left it in place (it still checks
something real) but added `test_simulate_actually_hits_the_cache`,
which asserts the actual `hits`/`misses`/`size` counts on a fresh
session, RED-proofed via `git stash` on `session.py` alone. Also added
`TestCachedRunner.test_base_params_override_changes_output` in
`test_infrastructure.py`, mirroring `SimulationRunner`'s own equivalent
test exactly.

likely raise: the `self._cached_runner._base_params = ...` sync line
runs outside `SimulationCache`'s own lock, so two threads calling

`PubMedFetcher.__init__` accepted a `fetch_full_text` param and the class
declared `EUROPE_PMC_URL`, and both the module and class docstrings
described full-text enrichment ("Full text, when available via Europe
PMC, is fetched transiently and passed to the extractor") -- but nothing
in `fetch_by_pubmed_id()` ever referenced either. Verified via grep
across the whole package: zero other references anywhere. This
specifically mattered to this project's own evidence-hierarchy
discipline: abstract-only access has repeatedly blocked real
investigations this session and earlier (`GLP1_MEAL_RESPONSE` anchoring,
the liraglutide benchmark, both explicitly logged as "confirmed

should actually be fetched.

Verified the real Europe PMC REST API by hand before writing any code
(not assumed from documentation): `search?query=EXT_ID:{pmid} AND
SRC:MED&format=json` returns `inEPMC`/`pmcid` for a given PMID;
`{pmcid}/fullTextXML` returns real JATS XML when `inEPMC == "Y"`.
Confirmed both branches with real PMIDs -- this session's own metformin
benchmark source (Hansen et al. 2024, PMID:39049802) is NOT open access
(`inEPMC: "N"`), while Shah et al. 2020 (PMID:32369480, PLoS One,
already cited for the steroid benchmark) IS (`inEPMC: "Y"`,
`pmcid: PMC7199958`) -- fetched its real ~15,000-character full text
successfully via the actual class before writing a single test.

the existing `_urlopen_https()` HTTPS-only helper and `_rate_limit()`),
extracts plain text from the JATS `<body>` via `"".join(body.itertext())`
(matches what `LLMExtractor.extract()` already expects -- it just
concatenates `paper.full_text` as plain text into a prompt). Best-effort
by design: any failure (not open access, no results, network error,

always documented as available only "for open-access papers", never a
guarantee, so `fetch_by_pubmed_id()`'s core abstract-based result must

### DONE — `ReproducibilityBundle.create_bundle()` now actually captures meals/drugs/personalization (follow-on to the `SimulationCache` collision entry, which deferred this)
Closed the gap noted (not fixed) during the `SimulationCache` fix
earlier this session: `create_bundle()` could only ever build
`scenario_dict={"name": output.scenario_name, "description":
output.scenario_description}` -- `SimulationOutput` never carried the
actual `ScenarioDefinition`, only those two strings, so meals, drugs,
and personalization were silently absent from every published bundle
despite the class's own docstring ("Everything needed to reproduce a
simulation result exactly") and the field's own comment
(`# ScenarioDefinition.to_dict()`) both implying otherwise.

Root cause was one level up from `create_bundle()` itself: the function
was never actually GIVEN the scenario, only the output. Fixed by adding
`SimulationOutput.scenario` (the `ScenarioDefinition` `SimulationRunner
.run()` actually executed, set at its one construction site in
`runner.py`) rather than changing `create_bundle()`'s signature to take
`scenario` as a second argument -- this avoids rippling the change
through `PlatformSession.bundle()` and every other caller, since the
scenario is now available directly from the object they already have.
`create_bundle()` falls back to the old `{"name", "description"}` shape
if `output.scenario` is `None` (hand-constructed `SimulationOutput`s
that don't set it), so nothing already relying on that shape breaks.

Checked before treating the new field as safe: `SimulationOutput
.summary()` (what `PrivacyAuditor.audit()` actually scans for raw
rsIDs) builds an explicit, curated dict and never touches
`self.scenario` at all -- adding this field doesn't create a new
privacy-audit blind spot.

**One real limitation, documented rather than silently accepted**: this
does NOT make `ReproducibilityBundle` fully live up to its "reproduce
exactly" claim for genetically-personalized scenarios specifically --
`to_dict()`'s `genetic_variant_fingerprints` (see the `SimulationCache`
entry above) are HMAC-keyed with a secret regenerated every process
start, precisely so they can't be reversed to a raw rsid. A bundle
archived by one process and read by a different one later can't
recover the exact original `Variant` from its fingerprint -- meals,
drugs, and physiological-profile personalization are now genuinely
reproducible from a bundle; the genetic dimension specifically isn't,
by design, and would need a separately-designed scheme to fix (noted in
`create_bundle()`'s own docstring, not attempted here).

+2 tests in `test_infrastructure.py` (`TestReproducibilityBundle`):
one confirms `bundle.scenario_dict` now actually contains
`meal_events`/`carbs_g` for the existing `high_sugar_meal_scenario()`
fixture; a second builds a scenario with drug events and a T2D
physiological profile from scratch and confirms both appear in the
bundle. RED-proofed via `git stash` across all three changed source
files together (`output.py`/`runner.py`/`infra.py` -- a single
indivisible fix, not separable). Full suite: 1312 -> 1314 passed,
2 skipped.

### DONE (partially) — `metformin_modifiers()`'s mechanism weighting corrected against gold-standard tracer evidence; `p3` left open (genuine literature conflict)
Follow-on to the metformin acute-meal-challenge benchmark above (model
undershoots the real postprandial iAUC effect by ~89%). Investigated
*why*, rather than stopping at "the model is too weak."

**What the model currently does** (`drug_interactions.py
::metformin_modifiers()`, citing Bailey & Turner 1996 NEJM review,
PMID:8569826): at max dose, `p3` (this model's Bergman-minimal-model
insulin-sensitivity/remote-insulin-action parameter, driving the `X`
compartment that multiplicatively scales glucose clearance) gets the
**largest** effect, +28%; `p1` (insulin-independent glucose
effectiveness) +10%; `Gb` (the basal glucose set point, the closest
proxy this model has for suppressed basal hepatic glucose production)
gets the **smallest**, -4%.

**Checked the cited source first, per this project's own discipline of
verifying what a citation actually says**: fetched PMID:8569826 via
`PubMedFetcher` -- it's a narrative NEJM review with no indexed
abstract/data at all (confirmed empty via the real API response, not
assumed). It cannot be the source of these specific percentages; they
were evidently illustrative estimates, not extracted from a table --
the same "uncited-in-practice" pattern this file has already caught and
fixed for other parameters (`DEFAULT_HEPATIC_EXTRACTION`, the original
wrong `p3` citation, etc.).

**Found real, quantitative, mechanism-specific evidence instead**:
searched PubMed for placebo-controlled metformin tracer/clamp studies,
verified via `PubMedFetcher`:
- **PMID:8923861** (Cusi/Consoli-style tracer study, *J Clin Endocrinol
  Metab* 1996): randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, n=20
  T2D + 8 controls, 15 weeks metformin vs. placebo, `[6-3H]glucose`
  tracer + euglycemic clamp -- the gold-standard method for separating
  hepatic vs. peripheral effects. Result: metformin reduced basal
  hepatic glucose production 12.9 -> 11.0 umol/kg.min (**-14.7%**,
  P<0.01), but **did NOT improve insulin-mediated total body glucose
  disposal at all** (10.9 vs. 11.0 umol/kg.min, P=NS) -- "neither
  oxidative nor nonoxidative glucose disposal was improved." No changes
  in the placebo arm. The paper's own conclusion: "the primary mechanism
  by which metformin improves glycemic control is... suppression of
  accelerated basal HGP," not peripheral insulin sensitivity.
- **PMID:1955512** (secondary, supporting, single-arm before/after, less
  rigorous): basal HGP fell 83 -> 61 mg/m2.min (**-26.5%**) over 3
  months of metformin 2.5g/day, correlated with the glycemic response --
  same direction, larger magnitude, but not placebo-controlled and
  confounded by 5kg weight loss in the obese subgroup.

**The apparent mismatch**: real evidence points to the hepatic/`Gb`
pathway as metformin's *dominant* mechanism (~15-27% reduction in HGP)
and essentially *no* effect on the `p3`/peripheral-insulin-sensitivity
pathway -- the model currently has this close to inverted (p3 the
biggest lever, Gb the smallest). If correct, re-weighting toward Gb and
away from p3 could plausibly close some or all of the benchmark's ~89%
undershoot -- but this is a hypothesis to verify by actually running
it, not a conclusion to act on yet.

**Returned to this in a later session pass, resolved what had clean
evidence, left what remains genuinely disputed**:

**`p1` -- fixed, removed entirely.** The missing literature check (item
2 above) was done: searched specifically for metformin's effect on
Bergman-model glucose effectiveness (S_G), found two independent,
placebo-controlled studies, both verified via `PubMedFetcher`:
**PMID:8582131** (double-blind, randomized, crossover, obese IGT
subjects, Bergman minimal-model IVGTT analysis): "AUC glucose, KG and
SG were similar in both tests" -- no significant change, while SI
(insulin sensitivity) *did* increase (see below). **PMID:16968813**:
"In contrast to metformin, pioglitazone improved... insulin-independent
glucose disposal [glucose effectiveness (S_G)]" -- i.e. metformin did
not. Convergent, unambiguous: removed `p1`'s uncited +10% entirely
(`compose_all_modifiers()`'s own documented behavior -- "parameters not
mentioned... keep a factor of 1.0" -- makes omission the correct way to
express "no effect", not a special-cased zero).

**`Gb` -- fixed, corrected -4% to -14.7%.** Directly anchored to
PMID:8923861's measured HGP reduction (item 1's flux-to-concentration
concern handled via an explicit, stated approximation: this model's
`Gb` is a steady-state concentration this simplified ODE sets directly
rather than deriving from a modeled production/clearance flux balance,
so absent a more principled translation, a given %-reduction in hepatic
production is assumed to produce approximately the same %-reduction in
the resulting basal concentration, holding clearance kinetics fixed --
labeled as an approximation to revisit, not presented as exact).

**`p3` -- was left open pending resolution; resolved in a later session
pass (see the "DONE -- Resolved the `p3` metformin conflict" entry
further down this document).** Summary: PMID:8923861 (chronic, 15wk,
T2D, gold-standard tracer/clamp) found *zero* peripheral improvement;
PMID:8582131 (acute, 2-day, obese IGT, also placebo-controlled) found a
*real* SI increase (6.98 vs. 4.61 x10^-5 min^-1 per pM, P=0.03).
Different populations (T2D vs. pre-diabetic obese), different durations
(chronic vs. acute) -- not resolvable by asking "which study is more
correct in general" (that really is an open question in the field, the
same category as the `for_gi()` GI-timing-slope limitation elsewhere in
this file). It WAS resolvable by asking a narrower, answerable question
instead: which regime does `metformin_modifiers()` itself represent?
See the later entry for the resolution.

**Full regression review (item 3), done properly, not skipped**: ran
the entire suite after each change. `p1`'s removal alone flipped the
metformin validation benchmark (above) from a small, correctly-directioned
undershoot (+20.66 mmol.min/L) to a small, WRONG-DIRECTION result
(-2.18 -- i.e. the model briefly said metformin slightly *raises*
postprandial glucose). Investigated why before accepting or reverting
either change, rather than assuming the direction flip meant the `p1`
fix was wrong: traced the actual simulated trajectories directly (drug
vs. placebo `PathwayParameters`, `glucose_iauc_4h_mmol_min_per_L`) --
confirmed `p1` was now correctly identical between arms (0.0317 both),
and the flip is a real, mechanistic consequence of `p1` also scaling
this ODE's insulin-independent clearance-rate term, not an unrelated
bug. Tested the `Gb` correction's effect on this same comparison before
committing to it (item 4's "check after deriving independently" order,
respected): with `Gb` at -14.7%, the reduction becomes **+9.07
mmol.min/L** -- correct direction restored. This is itself informative,
not just a fix: it's independent behavioral confirmation that `Gb`'s
old -4% really was substantially undersized, from a completely
different signal (the comparative 4h-iAUC benchmark) than the one used
to derive the new value (the tracer study), rather than two views of
the same measurement.

**Final, honestly-reported benchmark result** (item 4's actual check,
done last, not first): `ModelValidator().validate_metformin()` now
gives **model=9.07 mmol.min/L vs. real 186.0 (-95.1% deviation)** --
correctly directioned, but a *larger*-looking undershoot than the
pre-fix -88.9%. Same precedent as the semaglutide/steroid-double-count
entries elsewhere in this file: a scientifically correct fix can
honestly move a benchmark further from its reference, and that gets
disclosed, not hidden or reverted to preserve a better-looking number.
The qualitative conclusion is unchanged either way (this model's
`Gb`/`p3`-only representation of metformin cannot yet reproduce the
real drug's full acute postprandial effect) -- what changed is that the
remaining gap is now grounded in verified literature rather than an
uncited guess, and future work on `p3`'s genuine conflict is the next
concrete, well-scoped step, not a re-derivation from scratch.

+1 test (`test_metformin_has_no_p1_effect` in `test_physiology.py`,
RED-proofed via `git stash`); the two existing metformin-benchmark
tests (`test_metformin_genuinely_reduces_glucose_iauc`,
`test_model_currently_undershoots_the_real_effect`) failed transiently
after the `p1`-only change and pass again, unmodified, once `Gb` was
also corrected -- confirming both changes needed to land together, not
as two independent commits. Full suite: 1337 -> 1338 passed, 2 skipped.

**Mandatory security-reviewer pass (this touches drug-dosing
coefficients) found two real, worth-recording issues, both fixed or
disclosed**:
1. **Fixed**: three other files' comments (`hepatic.py`'s
   `for_metformin()` docstring, `test_hepatic.py`, `test_simulation_api.py`)
   still said "-4%" for the static Gb modifier -- the exact "same fact
   duplicated across files, nothing cross-checks it" bug class this
   session already fixed for `Vg_L_per_kg`/`MODEL_VERSION`/`gi_category`.
   Updated all three; none of their actual assertions depended on the
   specific magnitude (the hepatic fixed-point property they test is
   independent of it), so this was a documentation-only drift, not a
   second latent bug.
2. **Disclosed, not changed**: verified numerically that the corrected
   -14.7% Gb coefficient pushes `PhysiologicalPersonalizer`'s existing
   `MIN_GB_THRESHOLD_MARGIN_MM` safety clamp (added in an earlier
   session fix, guards `Gb` from collapsing too close to `G_threshold`)
   from a rare backstop into a routinely-engaged floor for realistic
   combinations -- confirmed directly: max-dose chronic metformin +
   moderate alcohol now composes to exactly the clamped `Gb=4.8mM`
   (`G_threshold=4.5` + the clamp's own 0.3mM margin) rather than its
   own distinct, unclamped value. The clamp's own regression tests still
   pass (this is safe, not a bug), but multiple distinct realistic
   combinations will now silently collapse to the identical clamped
   value instead of reflecting their relative intensity. Noted here so
   a future session investigating an unexpectedly-identical `Gb` across
   different scenarios finds the explanation immediately rather than
   re-discovering it. Also added an inline comment at the `0.147`
   literal itself (not just in the docstring above it) flagging it as
   an approximation, per the review's note that a bare numeric literal
   reads as more authoritative than a caveat several lines above it.

Revisited by asking a narrower, answerable question instead: which

`validate_metformin()`'s own docstring already states the model
"treats every metformin dose as the chronic, steady-state effect,"
unconditionally, regardless of `is_chronic`. And this platform's own
metformin validation benchmark (`validate_metformin()`, Hansen et al.
2024, PMID:39049802) is itself a **chronic (14-day), T2D-population**
trial -- the same regime as PMID:8923861 (chronic, T2D), not
PMID:8582131 (acute, pre-diabetic obese IGT). So while the two studies
may both be correct about their own respective regimes (this is not a
claim that PMID:8582131 is wrong or lower-quality), only one of those
regimes is the one `metformin_modifiers()` -- and this platform's own
benchmark -- actually claims to model. The applicable evidence for what
this function represents is PMID:8923861, which found no peripheral
effect.

Removed `p3`'s uncited +28% entirely (same disposition as `p1` in the
entry above, not a new precedent). **Checked the benchmark impact
honestly, in both directions, before and after removal** -- per this
project's own rule against curve-fitting to preserve a passing/better-
looking number: `validate_metformin()`'s deviation moved from -95.1%
(model 9.07 mmol.min/L) to **-97.6% (model 4.45 mmol.min/L)** vs. the
real 186.0 mmol.min/L reference -- a *larger*-looking undershoot, not a
smaller one. Still correctly directioned (a real, positive reduction,
not zero or reversed) and still WIDE-tolerance-gated (no effect on the
report's overall PASS verdict, same policy as every other WIDE miss in
this file). Disclosed as a real cost of a scientifically-justified fix,
not hidden or used as a reason to keep the uncited number -- the
existing `test_model_currently_undershoots_the_real_effect` test uses a
directional bound (`0 < model_value < reference`), not a fixed number,
so it required no change and still correctly holds.

+1 test (`test_metformin_has_no_p3_effect` in `test_physiology.py`,
mirroring `test_metformin_has_no_p1_effect`'s existing shape exactly,
RED-proofed via `git stash`); 2 existing tests updated to the corrected
semantics (`test_metformin_increases_p3` deleted/replaced by the new
test above; `test_applied_modifiers_metformin_lists_p3_and_gb_not_just_p3`
renamed to `test_applied_modifiers_metformin_lists_gb_only`, since Gb is
now the only parameter metformin_modifiers() touches). Full suite:
1353 -> 1353 passed, 2 skipped (net zero -- one test replaced, one
renamed and re-asserted, none net-added).

**What remains genuinely open, not closed by this fix**: this model's

proxy) plus the separately-modeled `HepGlucPathway` EGP coupling --
whether that two-mechanism representation can ever close a ~98%
undershoot against Hansen et al.'s measured acute 4h postprandial effect
without curve-fitting is a separate, larger question than this specific

### DONE — The highest-severity Boolean watchdog rule was never actually wired into any confidence score this platform has ever reported
Surfaced by a background scan of `ode-engine` -- the core physics engine,
the one package most scientifically consequential and, until this pass,
the one NOT yet freshly scanned this session for the "computed but
never wired" bug class every other package already got checked for.

`boolean_pathway.py`'s `WatchdogEngine`/`GlucoseInsulinBooleanPathway`
is a complete, correct, tested implementation of three physiological
consistency rules (its own docstring: "Replaces the basic watchdog in
system.py with a proper rule-based implementation"), the highest-
severity one (0.30) being `G_elevated -> I_elevated` -- "elevated
glucose should trigger insulin secretion," i.e. a broken beta-cell
response, the single failure mode most directly relevant to this
platform's own core T2D/impaired-secretion mission. Verified via grep
across the whole `packages/` tree: `WatchdogEngine`/
`GlucoseInsulinBooleanPathway` are referenced only by their own module
and their own test file -- never instantiated by `system.py`,
`runner.py`, or anywhere real code runs. Instead, `ODESystem
._run_watchdog()` hand-rolls a duplicate, incomplete implementation
with only the other two rules, at a flat 0.3-per-violation penalty
(not matching `WatchdogEngine`'s own deliberately differentiated
0.25/0.25/0.30 severities either). Every `SimulationOutput
.expert_metrics.overall_watchdog_confidence` this platform has ever
reported -- REST API, UI, everywhere -- was blind to exactly the
consistency check most worth having.

Fixed by adding the missing rule directly into `_run_watchdog()`
(porting `WatchdogEngine`'s exact severities), rather than swapping in
`WatchdogEngine` wholesale -- confirmed `WatchdogEngine.compute_state()`
uses fixed `y_internal[:6]` indexing (safe today only because
`runner.py::_build_pathway()` always puts `GlucoseInsulinPathway` first
in any `CompositePathway`), while `_run_watchdog()`'s existing
name-based species lookup (`_find_species_index`, tolerant of
`CompositePathway`'s "<pathway>.<species>" prefixing) is strictly more
robust and worth keeping.

**Verified the fix doesn't false-positive on normal physiology** --
this was the main risk (a rule that fires during the brief, entirely
normal window right after a meal where glucose has risen but insulin
hasn't caught up yet would be worse than no rule, crying wolf on every
healthy meal). Checked two ways: (1) ran real scenarios (light snack,
standard meal, high-sugar meal, fasted) through the actual `ODESystem`
myself -- zero flags in all of them, because insulin crosses its 150 pM
threshold at ~1.3 min while glucose doesn't cross 8.0 mM until ~6.7 min
(the `first_phase_gain` dynamic-secretion term, keyed to glucose's
*rate* of rise not just its level, responds fast enough to stay ahead);
(2) the mandatory security-reviewer pass independently reproduced the
same crossing-time trace and confirmed zero false positives at
realistic settings across the same four scenario types, while
confirming the rule correctly starts firing once `secretion_scale`
drops below ~0.20-0.25 -- genuine impairment, not normal lag. Also
reproduced a real T2D scenario (100g meal): rule fires 118/400
timepoints, reflecting sustained hyperglycemia persisting after insulin
has already cleared -- a real, clinically-meaningful signal, not noise.

**Real, disclosed consequence, not a defect**: the security review ran
this platform's actual production T2D scenario builders and found mean
watchdog confidence measurably lower than before this fix across the
board (e.g. `type2_diabetes_meal_scenario()` 75g: 0.878 mean/0.50 min,
107/400 flagged; 200g: 0.834 mean/138 flagged; T2D+hypothyroid+90yo:
0.811 mean/181 flagged) -- no test anywhere asserts a specific
confidence value for these (confirmed by grep, only generic 0-1 bound
checks exist), so nothing breaks mechanically, but this is a real,
visible behavior change surfaced through the REST API/UI for this
platform's own flagship T2D scenarios. If anything downstream (a
dashboard, an alert threshold, a published validation report) treats
"confidence" as roughly session-stable, this will look like a
regression to it even though it's the correct effect of closing a real
gap. Noted here so that's understood as intentional if it's ever asked
about. The review also confirmed the three rules are mutually exclusive
by construction (rules 1/2 require `I_elevated=True`, rule 3 requires
`I_elevated=False`), so confidence from this watchdog alone never drops
below 0.50 at a single timepoint -- no double-penalty risk.

**Not fixed, noted**: the per-rule severities (0.25/0.25/0.30), ported
from `WatchdogEngine` unchanged, are still an uncited design choice, not
literature-derived -- same status as the flat 0.3 they replaced, not a
regression, but worth flagging the same way this file already flags
other uncited internal calibration constants.

Two smaller, same-scan findings, both confirmed genuinely zero-impact
today (no production caller) and fixed anyway since they were small and
correct: `CouplingSpec.validate()` accepted a `target_inputs` parameter
but never checked `self.target_input` against it (a typo'd
`target_input` in pathway-extension wiring would never be caught) --
added the missing check. `GlucoseInsulinPathway.descriptor
.input_signals` listed only 6 of the 9 signals `dydt()` actually reads
(missing `p1_modifier`, `extra_g_clearance_modifier`,
`secretion_scale_modifier`) -- corrected to all 9.

+3 tests (`test_ode_engine.py`, `test_pathway_expansion.py` x2),
RED-proofed via `git stash` per source file. Full suite: 1334 -> 1337
passed, 2 skipped.

### DONE — Fifth instance of the false-reassurance narrative bug: `risk_score.py`'s "Peak glucose" indicator could call a WHO-borderline peak "a healthy response"
Follow-on scan of `lay-output`'s narrative-generation code specifically
for this bug class (four earlier instances this session: the mTOR/AMPK
indicator, the lay/report glucose narratives, and the risk-caveat
pipeline gap fixed above) -- confirmed those four are intact and this
is a genuinely new, fifth instance, not a re-report.

`compute_risk_profile()`'s "Peak glucose" indicator (`risk_score.py`)
gated its LOW/MODERATE bands purely on `excursion` (peak minus the
patient's OWN baseline), never on the absolute `peak_mM` -- only the
ELEVATED/HIGH bands checked absolute value against WHO thresholds, and
those were only reachable once `excursion >= 3.5`. For a patient whose
own baseline is already elevated (e.g. the T2D disease-state preset,
~6.5 mM), a small further rise landed the absolute peak squarely in the
WHO borderline/impaired-glucose-tolerance range (7.8-11.1 mM) while
still being called "a healthy response." Reproduced directly:
`type2_diabetes_meal_scenario(carbs_g=25)` -- baseline 6.5 mM, peak
8.4 mM (excursion 1.9, under the 2.0 cutoff) -> `RiskBand.LOW`, "a
healthy response." From the exact same `SimulationOutput`, `report.py`'s
own "Peak blood sugar" indicator (already correctly gated on absolute
value) calls the identical 8.4 mM "borderline range... reduced glucose
tolerance" -- two indicators computed from the same data, directly
contradicting each other.

Fixed by making the absolute WHO threshold the primary gate (matching
`report.py`'s already-correct logic), with excursion size only
distinguishing LOW vs. MODERATE within the genuinely-below-threshold
case, same as before this fix. +1 test, RED-proofed via `git stash`.
Full suite: 1341 -> 1342 passed, 2 skipped.

### DONE — `PersonalizationResult` was leaking real, raw rsIDs in two separate fields, despite its own docstring claiming otherwise -- caught in two passes, not one
Follow-on scan of `genotype` -- the last major package not freshly
re-scanned this session for the "computed but never wired" bug class
(it was covered by an *earlier* session's audit, not this one), chosen
specifically because it's the most privacy-sensitive package in the
platform (rule 7: "PersonalizationResult must never contain raw rsIDs
or allele data").

**Finding #1, verified directly**: `ComposedEffect.contributing_variants`
(a field on `PersonalizationResult.applied_effects`) stored raw `(rsid,
dosage)` tuples -- e.g. `[('rs7903146', 2)]` -- reproduced with a real
`GenotypePersonalizer().personalize(...)` call. Meanwhile
`PrivacyAuditor`'s checks meant to catch exactly this
(`hasattr(gp, 'variants')` in `audit()`, `hasattr(result,
'original_variants')` in `audit_personalization_result()`) were vacuous
no-ops -- neither attribute has ever existed on `PersonalizationResult`,
so both checks were structurally always `False` regardless of content,
reporting a false PASS on real leaking output. Fixed the same way as
`biosim_api.scenario`'s identical fix earlier this session: a keyed
HMAC fingerprint (`composer.py`'s `_rsid_fingerprint()`, independently
reimplemented rather than imported, since `biosim_genotype` sits below
`biosim_api` in the dependency direction) replaces the raw rsid in
`contributing_variants`. Confirmed via the security-reviewer pass that
this platform's own `VariantEffectDB` has exactly the small (~14 rsID)
catalog that makes an *unkeyed* hash dangerous (same reasoning as the
original fix) -- keying closes it. Fixed `PrivacyAuditor`'s two vacuous
checks to actually inspect `applied_effects[*].contributing_variants`.

**Finding #2, caught by the mandatory security-reviewer pass on finding
#1, not by this pass independently**: `composer.py`'s population-mismatch
warning (`f"{record.rsid} ({record.gene}): effect size derived from
{population}..."`) embedded the raw rsid AND gene name directly --
sitting in the exact same functions this pass had just touched, but a
different field (`ComposedEffect.population_warnings`, not
`contributing_variants`). This one is more clearly *live*, not just
latent: `population_warnings` flows `PersonalizationResult
.population_warnings` -> (`runner.py`) `SimulationOutput.warnings` ->
the REST API's response verbatim (`schemas.py`'s `warnings: list[str]`).
The new Check 3 above never looked at it (it only scanned
`contributing_variants`), and `PersonalizationResult.summary()` only
exposes `any_population_warnings` (a bool), so the existing
`_contains_rsid`-on-`summary()` checks never saw the actual text either.
Mitigating factor confirmed by the reviewer: `SimulationRunner.run()`
never passes a non-default `user_population` today (so the mismatch
branch can't currently fire in production), and the REST API doesn't
yet accept genetic variants/ancestry as input -- not exploitable over
HTTP *today*, but `audit_personalization_result()` is the documented API
for any non-REST caller, and it silently passed real, raw genetic
identifiers.

Fixed at the source (data minimisation, not just detection): the warning
now names the affected model parameter (e.g. `"secretion_scale: effect
size derived from EUR population..."`) instead of the rsid/gene,
trading away per-variant attribution when multiple contributing records
share a parameter -- the correct trade-off given rule 7. Added a second
defense-in-depth backstop in `PrivacyAuditor` (`audit()`'s new Check 5,
`audit_personalization_result()`'s equivalent) scanning
`population_warnings` and `output.warnings` directly, since a "detect
after the fact" check is only a backstop, not a substitute for not
leaking at the source -- this is why finding #2 existed right next to
finding #1's fix and still wasn't caught until an adversarial review
asked "does this actually close the leak class, or just the one vector
it targeted?"

**Finding #3, same scan, unrelated to privacy**: `EffectRecord
.uncertainty_contribution` computed `abs(effect_se / effect_per_allele)
* abs(effect_per_allele)` -- the division and multiplication cancel
exactly for any nonzero `effect_per_allele`, so this always just
returned `effect_se` unchanged. `effect_se` is documented as "standard
error of effect_per_allele" -- the same units as `effect_per_allele`,
which is a genuine fraction for `MULTIPLICATIVE` records but an
absolute value (mM, nM) for `ADDITIVE_ABSOLUTE` records (Gb,
`G_threshold`, `IGF1b`). Composed downstream as a dimensionless CV in
quadrature with the tier-based CV -- a real unit-consistency bug,
currently low-impact only because the affected `effect_se` magnitudes
are small relative to typical tier CVs. Fixed by removing the erroneous
extra multiplication (the bare division is the correct fractional CV
for both effect types).

+7 tests total (`test_genotype.py` x5, `test_infrastructure.py` x2), all
RED-proofed via `git stash`. Full suite: 1345 -> 1351 passed, 2 skipped.

### DONE — `IDRegistry`'s merge workflow left deprecated entities' data permanently stale in two ways
Follow-on scan of `id-resolver`/`curation` -- the last two packages not
freshly re-scanned this session (both were last fixed in an *earlier*
session: df0d133's collision-check exemption and b6d6baf's conflict_id
ordering fix, both older than this session's starting commit). Chosen
specifically because a merge-workflow bug in the canonical ID registry
would compound silently across the whole platform (everything resolves
through it). `curation` came back clean -- traced every consumer
(`biosim_uncertainty.curation_bridge`, data-seeds integration tests),
nothing beyond the already-fixed conflict_id issue.

`IDRegistry.register()`'s merge/deprecation path (the workflow df0d133
made functional last session) only re-points the cross-references
**explicitly restated** in the merging call, and never removes the
deprecated entity's own entry from the internal canonical index.
Verified directly with a real `register()`/merge sequence, not just
code reading:

1. **`resolve()` can silently return a deprecated `CanonicalID`.**
   Register an entity with HMDB+KEGG cross-references, then merge it
   into a new entity that only restates HMDB (a realistic case --
   restating every cross-reference an entity ever accumulated is easy
   to forget). `resolve()` for the KEGG accession still returned the
   OLD (deprecated) canonical ID, silently -- `resolve()` never
   consults the deprecated-ID index at all, only `get_record()` does,
   so nothing on this path even mentions "deprecated." This directly
   violates `types.py`'s own module-level promise: "Every biological
   entity in the platform has exactly one canonical ID."
2. **`stats()` permanently double-counts every merged-away entity.**
   Its own docstring says "for monitoring and health checks" --
   confirmed directly: merging one entity into another left
   `total_entities` at 2, not 1, and this compounds with every future
   merge.

Both were latent rather than live in production today (confirmed via
grep: no caller in `data-seeds` uses `deprecated_canonical_ids` yet) --
but now that df0d133 made merges actually succeed, this bookkeeping gap
is exactly what a real caller hits next. Fixed by (1) auto-inheriting
every cross-reference the deprecated entity actually had into the new
entity's record before the existing collision-check/index-rebuild logic
runs, rather than requiring the caller to manually restate everything
the old entity owned, and (2) removing the deprecated entity's stale
entry from the canonical index at merge time (safe: `get_record()`
already checks the deprecated index first and never falls through to a
stale entry there, so this was pure dead weight inflating `stats()`).

+2 tests in `TestDeprecation`, RED-proofed via `git stash`. Full suite:
1351 -> 1353 passed, 2 skipped.

### DONE — REST API's `MealEventIn` wire schema was missing `glycaemic_index`/`kabs` entirely
Direct follow-on to the earlier `DrugEventIn.hours_before_simulation`
fix (same bug shape, meals instead of drugs): `MealEvent`
(`scenario.py`) has had `glycaemic_index`/`kabs` fields since KNOWN BUGS
FIXED #15 (the `gi_meals` kabs-wiring fix), used to route to the
literature-calibrated `GutAbsorptionModel` instead of the default
monoexponential absorption -- but `MealEventIn` (the REST wire schema)
never gained either field, and `scenario_in_to_definition()` never set
them when constructing the internal `MealEvent`. A REST client could
never submit a GI-adjusted meal at all; every meal submitted via
`POST /simulate` silently got the default absorption shape regardless
of the food's real glycaemic index.

Fixed: added `glycaemic_index: Optional[float] = Field(default=None,
ge=0, le=100)` and `kabs: Optional[float] = Field(default=None, gt=0)`
to `MealEventIn`, threaded through in `scenario_in_to_definition()`.
The `0-100` bound matches `MealEvent`'s own documented range and is
consistent with `GutAbsorptionModel.for_gi()`'s own internal clamp
(`max(10.0, min(100.0, glycaemic_index))`) -- checked directly, not
assumed, before picking that constraint. `MealEvent.__post_init__`'s
existing mutual-exclusivity check (can't set both) is already caught by
`/simulate`'s existing `except ValueError -> HTTPException(400)`, no
route change needed.

+2 tests (`test_meal_event_glycaemic_index_actually_applies`,
`test_meal_event_rejects_both_glycaemic_index_and_kabs`), RED-proofed
via `git stash` -- both failed as expected without the fix (identical
peak times across GI=100/GI=30, confirming GI was silently dropped;
200 instead of 400, confirming the validation never reached the
model). Full suite: 1353 -> 1355 passed, 2 skipped.

**Review-process note**: the mandatory code-reviewer pass hit the same
session-quota outage documented earlier this session ("resets 12:50am
Europe/London") -- not a finding. Did not retry (would fail
identically); performed the equivalent verification directly instead:
confirmed the `/simulate` route's existing `ValueError -> 400` handling
needed no change, confirmed both tests are genuine (RED-proofed, not
tautological), and confirmed the Pydantic bounds match both
`MealEvent`'s docstring and `for_gi()`'s own internal clamp rather than
being an arbitrary guess.

### DONE — Fixed the PubMedFetcher abstract-truncation bug (Track 1, first milestone under the new strategic roadmap)

Follow-on to the bug flagged in the Session close note above.
`PubMedFetcher._parse_pubmed_xml()` (`fetcher.py`) built `abstract` from
`(el.text or "")` per `<AbstractText>` element -- in `ElementTree`,
`.text` returns only the text up to the FIRST child element, so any
abstract containing inline markup (`<sub>`, `<i>` -- common for
subscripted units like Tm<sub>G</sub> or italicized P-values) was
silently truncated right at that tag, with no error or warning.

Fixed: replaced `(el.text or "")` with `"".join(el.itertext())` per
`AbstractText` element, which recursively concatenates all text
including nested elements' content. The join across multiple
`AbstractText` elements (structured abstracts) is unchanged.

Regression test (`test_abstract_with_inline_markup_is_not_truncated`,
`TestPubMedFetcherParsing`) uses a fixture built from the REAL
`<Abstract>` XML block, fetched live from NCBI efetch for PMID:28428225
during this session (not paraphrased/invented) -- the exact paper where
the bug was originally discovered. RED-proofed via `git stash` on
`fetcher.py` only: the test fails against the pre-fix code at exactly
the documented truncation point (309 characters, cut off at
"...maximal renal glucose transport (Tm"), then passes once the stash
is popped. Full suite: 1355 -> 1356 passed, 2 skipped.

**Code-reviewer pass**: ran clean, no quota issue this time. Verdict:
APPROVE, 0 findings across all severities. Confirmed independently: fix
correctness (`itertext()` is the right replacement, no tail-text-loss
edge case, multi-`AbstractText` join behavior unchanged), regression
test genuineness (fails at the exact documented failure mode against
the pre-fix code, not a tautological assertion), and no new `ruff`
findings introduced by the diff. Not drug/dosage/physiology/genetics/
calculation code, so no security-reviewer pass required per the
project's standing rule.

This unblocks leaning on `literature-curator` for citation verification
work going forward (the abstract text it reads is now trustworthy for
papers with inline markup) -- see the SGLT2i pathway milestone next.

### DONE — Built the SGLT2-inhibitor renal glucose clearance pathway (Track 1, second milestone)

The first insulin-INDEPENDENT drug mechanism this platform models
(dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) -- new files `packages/ode-engine/src/
biosim_ode/renal_pathway.py` (`RenalClearanceParameters`, `RenalPathway`,
`renal_couplings()`/`couple_with_gi()`) plus a new rule-11 signal
`renal_glucose_clearance_delta` wired into `GlucoseInsulinPathway.dydt()`.

**Design question resolved first, before writing pathway code** (per the
Session close note's open flag): used `computational-biologist` to
scope the mechanism, then independently verified its one NEW citation
live (PMID:23735727, DeFronzo et al. 2013, *Diabetes Care* 36(10):
3169-76, PMCID:PMC3781504 -- fetched full text via Europe PMC and
cross-checked every specific number the agent quoted against it directly:
GFR 127/128 mL/min, TmG 317/420/349 mg/min, appearance thresholds
9.5/10.9 mM, splay AUCs, the "162 g/day"/"~375 mg/min"/"24-h urine
glucose excretion (60-80 g/day)... 40-50% of filtered glucose load"
quotes -- all matched exactly). **Answer: SGLT2i does NOT get metformin's
two-part (static Gb modifier + zero-at-basal dynamic pathway) design.**
Unlike metformin's insulin-gated hepatic suppression (genuinely ~0 at
basal insulin), SGLT2i's renal clearance is continuously active whenever
glucose exceeds the drug-lowered threshold -- and normal fasting glucose
(~5mM) is already above that threshold (<2mM per both source papers).
Forcing the pathway to be zero at basal would zero out the drug's actual
mechanism. Adding a static Gb modifier alongside it would double-count
exactly the way `CortisolPathway`/`glucocorticoid_modifiers()` once did
(see KNOWN BUGS). So: **the ODE pathway is the sole representation** --
`_sglt2_inhibitor_modifiers()` (`drug_interactions.py`) returns `{}`,
matching `_glp1_agonist_modifiers()`'s existing precedent exactly, not a
new pattern.

**Mechanism**: a smooth Tm-limited renal reabsorption model (not a hard
threshold -- DeFronzo's own measured 9.5mM appearance threshold is well
below the 14.1mM a hard Tm/GFR cutoff would imply, falsifying that
simpler model), `R(F) = (1-beta)*F*hill_inhibition(F, Tm, p)**(1/p)`,
reusing the existing `hill_inhibition` kinetics primitive (verified this
is the correct rewrite of the smooth-min form: `hill_inhibition(x,ic50,n)
= 1/(1+(x/ic50)^n)`, matches `[1+(F/Tm)^p]^(-1/p)` exactly). `beta`
(concentration-independent reabsorption-capacity loss, representing the
threshold collapse) is the one genuinely new free parameter, derived
(not measured) from PMID:23735727's own "60-80 g/day, 40-50% of filtered
load" statement via a documented "glucose held at fasting all day"
approximation (beta=0.40 -- verified this reproduces 66 g/day at fasting
glucose, squarely in the quoted range). Splay index p=8 is an inferred
shape parameter (DeFronzo's own splay AUC integral is in Supplementary
Data, not retrievable via Europe PMC this session) -- both flagged
explicitly as approximations in the module docstring, not presented as
measured.

**Architectural finding, verified directly against `coupling.py`**:
`CompositePathway.dydt()` computes every sub-pathway's `output_signals()`
from ONLY that pathway's own state slice, before any signal injection --
so no existing pathway (hepatic/GLP1/cortisol/exercise) had ever needed
to export a signal that's a function of ANOTHER pathway's instantaneous
state. `RenalPathway` is the first one that does (needs glucose). Solved
by giving it one real state variable (the clearance-delta itself)
relaxing toward a target computed inside `dydt()` (which DOES receive
injected signals) from an injected `glucose_mM` signal -- same
input-signal -> internal-target -> relaxing-state -> output-signal shape
`HepGlucPathway` already uses for insulin, just with the direction of
"which pathway's state feeds which" reversed. `y0` is the fixed point at
`GLUCOSE_REFERENCE_MM` (5.0, matching `PathwayParameters.Gb`'s own
default) -- exactly zero when beta=0, genuinely negative when a drug
preset is active (this is a STRONGER neutrality guarantee than
`hepatic_egp_delta`: exactly zero at every glucose value, not just at
one reference point, since the no-drug case must produce zero
regardless of what glucose value it's evaluated at).

**Two-part design resolved a second time, for the presets**: no dose
scaling (unlike `for_metformin(dose_mg)`) -- the verified data varies by
treatment DURATION, not dose (`for_dapagliflozin()`: fixed 7-day preset;
`for_empagliflozin(days_of_treatment)`: interpolates beta between the
two confirmed timepoints, 48h and day 14, clamped to that measured
range, no extrapolation). Canagliflozin gets no preset at all (per
`computational-biologist`'s explicit recommendation) -- its own abstract
confirms a confounding intestinal SGLT1 mechanism this platform doesn't
model, so calibrating renal parameters against it would fold a
non-renal effect into a renal-only model.

**Validation benchmark**: `ModelValidator.validate_sglt2i()` against
Polidori et al. 2013 (PMID:23412078, canagliflozin vs. placebo, same
meal) -- WIDE tolerance, and the model is EXPECTED to undershoot (4.25%
vs. 35% reference glucose-AUC reduction; 7.33% vs. 43% insulin-AUC
reduction), documented explicitly in both the benchmark dataset's
docstring and the validator method's own docstring, not silently
accepted or curve-fit to force a pass -- same honesty standard as
`validate_semaglutide()`'s documented overshoot and
`validate_metformin()`'s documented undershoot.

**Review-process note, said honestly**: BOTH the mandatory code-reviewer
and security-reviewer passes hit a session-quota outage ("resets 6am
Europe/London") within moments of each other. Did not retry identically
(would fail the same way) -- performed the equivalent verification
directly instead, and it surfaced two real, previously-unfound bugs in
code from this same milestone (not the pre-existing codebase):
1. `RenalClearanceParameters.for_empagliflozin(days_of_treatment=nan)`
   silently resolved to the day-14 beta with no error at all -- `max()`/
   `min()`-based clamping treats NaN as "not less than" whatever it's
   compared against first, since NaN comparisons are always False.
   Fixed: reject non-finite `days_of_treatment` explicitly.
2. `target_delta_mM_per_min()` raised an uncaught `OverflowError` for a
   sufficiently extreme glucose value (`x**n` overflowing float64 inside
   `hill_inhibition`), and silently produced a NaN for `glucose_mM=inf`
   (`inf * 0.0`) with no error at all -- either could propagate from a
   single divergent upstream ODE state, not just a deliberately
   adversarial input. Fixed with a defensive upper clamp
   (`GLUCOSE_UPPER_BOUND_MM = 150.0`, far beyond any physiologically
   real glucose value -- the highest documented human case is ~147 mM --
   so this cannot affect any realistic simulated scenario).
Both fixed with their own regression test, both RED-proofed directly
(temporarily reverting just the new lines, confirming the exact failure
mode, then restoring) rather than via a whole-file `git stash` (both
fixes landed inside the same new, not-yet-committed file as the feature
itself). Also ran `ruff` and `bandit` manually on every changed file as
a substitute for the automated passes: `ruff` findings on the new file
are the same pre-existing style conventions already present in sibling
files (`hepatic.py`, `glp1_pathway.py` have the identical finding types
at higher counts) -- not new problems; `bandit` found one Low-severity
false positive on pre-existing, untouched code (`ValidationVerdict.PASS
= "PASS"` misidentified as a hardcoded password string), nothing in the
actual diff.

+43 tests across `test_renal_pathway.py` (new), `test_pathway_expansion.py`,
`test_physiology.py`, `test_simulation_api.py`, `test_validation.py`,
`test_rest_api.py`. Full suite: 1356 -> 1399 passed, 2 skipped.
